The table also shows why the two measures should not be averaged or blended. They answer different questions, and the gap between them is itself information: it is a rough index of how cheap non-traded goods and services are in an economy relative to the reference. As economies converge in income, their price levels tend to rise towards those of richer economies and the gap narrows — so part of what the market-rate series records as convergence over a long period is the closing of the price gap, not only growth in volume. The PPP numbers are also revised whenever the International Comparison Program publishes a new round of price surveys, so an analyst who quotes “China passed the United States in 2014” is quoting a particular vintage of price data, and should say so (World Bank 2026).
The third decision is about who is in the denominator. The world total is a World Bank aggregate that includes economies for which data are sparse or estimated, particularly in the early decades, and not every member of the Industrialising Six is present throughout. Poland has no GDP figure in the series before 1990: for the first twenty years of the period, the Six are in fact five. A stacked chart of shares — G7, I6, rest of the world — therefore shows the “rest of the world” absorbing whatever is missing from the Six, which is an artefact of the data, not a fact about the world.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.7 From convergence to backlash
text:
2.7 From convergence to backlash
The convergence was, by most measures of global welfare, a remarkable success. It was also politically destabilising in the countries whose share was shrinking, and the most useful framework for understanding why comes from Dani Rodrik.

Rodrik’s trilemma — the proposition that a country can have at most two of three things: deep economic integration with the world economy, national sovereignty in policy-making, and democratic politics (Rodrik 2011).

The logic is that deep integration requires harmonised rules — on products, on investment, on capital flows — and those rules constrain what national governments can do. If the nation-state keeps its sovereignty and pursues deep integration, democratic choice must be constrained: governments adopt whatever policies markets reward, a condition Rodrik describes with Thomas Friedman’s phrase, the “golden straitjacket”. If integration and democracy are both kept, the rules must be made democratically above the state — a global federalism no one has built. If sovereignty and democracy are kept, integration must be shallow: the Bretton Woods compromise, with managed openness and room for national policy.
The trilemma is a reading of the history in the previous sections. Embedded liberalism was the third option: shallow integration that left room for democracy and sovereignty. The neoliberal turn and the WTO pushed towards deep integration — Rodrik calls it hyperglobalisation — and, for a while, the countries concerned accepted the straitjacket. The backlash of the 2010s and 2020s — Brexit, the tariff wars that began in 2018, the return of industrial policy, export controls, investment screening, “de-risking” — can be read as a sequence of choices of sovereignty and democracy over deep integration.
The economics behind the politics became clearer with evidence on the distribution of the gains. Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013) showed that US local labour markets more exposed to rising Chinese import competition after 2000 suffered larger falls in manufacturing employment and wages, and higher take-up of public transfers, with effects that persisted. What the “China shock” literature showed was that the losers were geographically concentrated, that adjustment was slow, and that the compensation the embedded-liberal bargain had promised did not reach them. A bargain that is not honoured stops being a bargain.

2.7.1 Slowbalisation
The phenomenon that the press calls slowbalisation is visible in a single series, world trade as a percentage of world GDP, drawn in the left panel of Figure 2.4. It was about 26 per cent in 1970 and 38 per cent in 1990, and peaked at about 60 per cent in 2008; it fell to 52 per cent in 2009 and has oscillated since between the low fifties and 62 per cent, reached in 2022, a year of high commodity prices. The last year in the release jumps to well above any earlier value, but it rests on reports from 138 economies, against 183 for 2022, and should be read as provisional. Whether the flattening is a retreat from globalisation or a change in its form is contested. A retreat would show up as firms reshoring and supply chains shortening; a change of form, as trade in goods stagnating while poorly measured trade in services and data continues to grow. The series alone cannot settle the question, because its denominator, GDP, has shifted towards services, which are traded less, in exactly the period in question.






Figure 2.4: World trade rose from 26 per cent of world GDP in 1970 to 60 per cent in 2008 and has moved sideways since; net inflows of foreign direct investment peaked at 5.3 per cent of world GDP in 2007 and were near 1 per cent in 2023–2025. Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS, BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS), world aggregates; the last trade observation is provisional.



The right panel tells a starker story, and it is the one closer to the multinational’s own decisions. Net inflows of foreign direct investment — the money firms commit to owning and controlling operations abroad — were under 1 per cent of world GDP until the late 1980s, rose to 4.6 per cent in 2000 and 5.3 per cent in 2007, waves of cross-border mergers riding the second unbundling, and have since fallen back. They averaged 3.3 per cent of world GDP in 2000–2007 and 1.6 per cent from 2018, with a low of 0.9 per cent in 2023: the level of the early 1990s. The series is noisy, because it records financial flows rather than factories — the 2018 trough reflects American multinationals repatriating foreign earnings after the 2017 US tax reform (UNCTAD 2019), and much FDI passes through holding companies in low-tax jurisdictions (Damgaard, Elkjaer, and Johannesen 2024) — but the direction is not in doubt. Trade has plateaued; the investment that builds supply chains has retreated. If slowbalisation is a change of form, it is one in which firms keep trading through the networks they built while becoming much more reluctant to build new ones abroad.


2.7.2 The dispute mechanism
One institutional fact belongs in every firm’s risk register. The WTO’s Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019, when the terms of its members expired and the United States blocked the appointment of replacements. A panel ruling can now be appealed “into the void”, where no body exists to hear it, and so never become binding. For a firm, a discriminatory measure by a trading partner is now more likely to be resolved by bargaining or retaliation between governments than by a legal ruling — by power rather than by procedure.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.8 Interdependence as an instrument
text:
2.8 Interdependence as an instrument
The first two parts of this chapter describe an order designed to make interdependence safe. The third must add that interdependence was never only an economic fact. Albert Hirschman, writing in 1945 about Nazi Germany’s trade with south-eastern Europe, showed that trade relations could be structured deliberately to create dependence: by trading with small partners for whom the trade was a large share of their total, a great power could make the threat of interrupting it a source of political influence (Hirschman 1945). The gains from trade, in his account, were also the measure of the power the trade conferred — the cost a partner would bear if it stopped.
Farrell and Newman (2019) brought the argument into the age of networks. The infrastructure of globalisation — financial messaging, dollar clearing, internet backbones, cloud platforms — is not flat; it has hubs, and the hubs sit disproportionately in a few jurisdictions. States that control the hubs can use them for surveillance, observing what flows through, and for exclusion, cutting adversaries off. Interdependence, on this reading, has been “weaponised”: the very networks that the economic order built become instruments of coercion. Chapters 8, 10 and 11 develop the argument for cyber, sanctions and space. Its relevance here is that the order’s openness and its vulnerability are the same thing seen from two sides.
For a multinational, the practical form of weaponised interdependence is jurisdictional reach. A firm that clears payments in dollars, stores data with a provider headquartered in one country, or uses components containing technology controlled by another, has placed part of its operations under that country’s law, wherever the firm itself is incorporated and wherever the transaction takes place. The order built after 1945 made it natural to route business through American banks, platforms and technology; the same routing now carries American regulatory authority with it, and China and the European Union have begun to build their own instruments of reach. A firm’s exposure is therefore a matter not only of where it sells and produces, but of which networks it runs through and whose law travels along them.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.9 What it means for the multinational
text:
2.9 What it means for the multinational
The history and the economics lead to four implications for a firm’s strategy.
The market is no longer where the rules are written. For most of the post-war period, the largest markets and the rule-makers were the same countries. The convergence separated them. A European firm now earns a growing share of its revenue in markets whose governments did not design the WTO, did not participate in Bretton Woods, and do not feel bound by the spirit — as distinct from the letter — of rules they joined late. The firm’s legal environment and its commercial environment have come apart.
The supply chain is a geopolitical object. If the second unbundling moved know-how along supply chains, then supply chains are where governments now intervene to stop it: export controls, outbound investment screening, restrictions on technology transfer, requirements to locate certain stages of production in trusted jurisdictions. The question for the firm is no longer only where a stage is cheapest, but where it is permitted, and by whom.
Multilateral protection is weaker. With the Appellate Body unable to hear appeals, the guarantee that a trading partner’s discriminatory measure could be challenged and removed through procedure has weakened. Firms that relied implicitly on that guarantee — exporters into markets with a history of trade remedies, for example — face disputes settled more often by negotiation and retaliation. The firm’s government’s bargaining power has become part of the firm’s risk profile.
Measurement choices are strategy choices. At market exchange rates the G7 still produces nearly half of world output; at PPP, little more than a quarter; and within the G7 the American share has held while Japan’s and Europe’s have shrunk. A risk analyst’s first duty is to show both measures, and the members, and say which question each answers.
Mapped onto the five channels of this book, the order’s transformation runs mainly through market access — the tariffs, trade remedies and bloc-based diversion of Chapter 4 — and through inputs, where the know-how and components that the second unbundling dispersed are now subject to control. But it reaches finance and payments too, because the dollar-centred monetary system that survived 1971 is the platform on which financial sanctions operate.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.10 What the figure does not license
text:
2.10 What the figure does not license
Baldwin’s figure is a powerful image, and its power is a reason for care. It does not license four conclusions that boards and commentators routinely draw from it.
A falling G7 share is relative. The G7 economies kept growing in absolute terms through the whole period; the denominator grew faster. A falling share does not mean the G7 market shrank, and a firm selling into the G7 did not lose customers because the line went down.
At current US dollars, the share moves with the dollar: a reading in any single year can say as much about currency markets as about convergence.
Convergence is concentrated. Most of the gain went to a handful of economies, and above all to China. “The South” did not converge; specific economies that joined specific supply chains did.
It shows income, not rule-making power. Whether a shrinking share of world GDP means a shrinking ability to set the rules is a question about the relation between economic size and political influence — the subject of Chapter 3. Hegemonic stability theory predicts that it does; institutionalists predict that rules can outlast the share. The chart cannot settle the dispute, because it does not measure the thing in dispute.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.11 A short review of the literature
text:
2.11 A short review of the literature

The political economy of the post-war order begins with the hegemonic-stability debate. Kindleberger (1973) attributed the interwar collapse to the absence of a stabilising power; Krasner (1976) generalised the argument to the structure of trade; Keohane (1984) replied that institutions can sustain cooperation after hegemony. Ruggie (1982) named the domestic bargain — embedded liberalism — on which post-war openness rested, and Ikenberry (2011) reinterpreted the American-led order as liberal, institutional and self-binding, and therefore “easy to join and hard to overturn”. The monetary history, from Bretton Woods through the end of gold convertibility, is told by Eichengreen (2019).
The economics of the new globalisation is organised by Baldwin (2016) around falling costs of moving goods, ideas and people, with the multinational’s supply chain as the conduit for the second unbundling; Baldwin and Lopez-Gonzalez (2015) map the regional structure of supply-chain trade. The distributional consequences in the rich countries are documented most influentially by Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013), and their political consequences are read through Rodrik (2011)’s trilemma of integration, sovereignty and democracy.
A third strand treats economic interdependence as a source of power rather than only of gains. Hirschman (1945) showed how asymmetric trade could be designed to create political dependence; Farrell and Newman (2019) extended the argument to the networked infrastructure of finance and communications, introducing “weaponised interdependence” — the strand that Chapters 8, 10 and 11 follow.
The through-line is that every account of the order answers the same question — what holds the rules in place — and that the answers differ chiefly in how much weight they give to the distribution of power. The great convergence is the event that puts that weight to the test.

title: 2  The International Economic Order: Who Wrote the Rules, and What Happens When Their Share Shrinks
section: 2.12 Whether the rules follow the income
text:
2.12 Whether the rules follow the income
The international economic order was written by a small number of states, at a moment when they held most of the world’s gold, most of its industry and, by the time the series begins, two-thirds of its output. The rules they wrote were multilateral in form, and in several layers they were written with the help of the firms that would live under them. Those rules made the second unbundling possible: they made it cheap and safe for a multinational to move know-how across borders inside its own production network, and the movement of know-how is what produced the convergence. The order, in this sense, financed its own relative decline — which is not a failure of design, since an open order was always going to spread industry to the places it reached.
What the data cannot say is whether the rules will follow the income. The G7’s share of world output has fallen from about two-thirds to well under half at market prices, and to little more than a quarter at purchasing-power parity. The institutions the G7 built are still standing: the Fund and the Bank still lend, the WTO’s schedules still bind tariffs, the dollar still clears most of the world’s trade. But some of what made them work has already gone. The Appellate Body cannot sit. The embedded-liberal bargain no longer holds in the countries that wrote it. And the networks through which goods, money and data move have become instruments of the states that host their hubs.
Two readings of that evidence compete. On the hegemonic-stability reading, rules that rested on the power of their authors will be revised as that power shrinks, and the revision is already under way — in tariffs, in export controls, in the rival institutions that rising states have begun to build. On the institutionalist reading, rules that are costly to abandon and useful to everyone will outlast the share of those who wrote them, and what looks like decline is a change of form, as in 1971. The evidence of the last decade supports neither reading cleanly. The order has changed form without collapsing; it has also lost two of the things that made it an order rather than a set of habits.
For a multinational, the practical consequence is that the rules can no longer be treated as a constant in the business plan. A firm that built its supply chain on the assumption of non-discriminatory tariffs, procedural dispute settlement and neutral financial networks built it on rules that were held in place by a particular distribution of power. A falling G7 share does not tell the firm that its G7 customers are poorer, that emerging markets in general are richer, or that the rules it relies on have already changed. It tells it that the economies that wrote the rules now produce a much smaller share of the world’s income than when they wrote them, and that the question of what holds the rules in place — which the next chapter answers from the realist side — has become a question about the firm’s own operations.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
text:
3.1 A system with no government
The previous chapter described the international economic order as a set of rules, written by particular states and held in place by something. This chapter asks what that something is when it is not law. Inside a country, a contract is enforced by courts, and the courts are backed by a state that holds a monopoly of legitimate force. Between countries there is no such state. There is no world government that can make a rule binding, enforce a contract between two governments, or guarantee that a state which disarms will not be invaded. That absence is the starting point of the realist tradition in international relations, and it is the reason this book cannot treat geopolitics as a branch of regulation.
The question that follows is direct. In a system with no government above states, who sets the terms of trade — and how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting? The realist answer to the first half is blunt: the terms are set, in the end, by those who hold the capabilities others need, and they are revised when the distribution of capabilities changes. The second half is a measurement problem, and the chapter answers it with two centuries of data on the distribution of material capabilities among the major powers, asking when, and on what measure, China overtook the United States.
The chapter defines anarchy; sets out the defensive and offensive realist theories; turns to power transition theory and Graham Allison’s “Thucydides’s Trap”; and examines how power is measured, and what the standard measure rewards and misses.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.2 Anarchy, and what it does not mean
text:
3.2 Anarchy, and what it does not mean

Anarchy — in international relations, the absence of any authority above states capable of making binding rules, enforcing agreements between them, or guaranteeing their survival. It describes the structure of the system, not the level of violence within it.

The word is a trap for newcomers, because in ordinary language it means chaos. In realist theory it means nothing of the kind. Most of the time, most states are at peace with most others; they trade, sign treaties, join organisations and settle disputes by negotiation. Anarchy is compatible with all of that. What it denies is that any of it is guaranteed by a higher authority. A treaty is kept because the parties find it in their interest to keep it, not because a court can compel them; a trading relationship continues because both sides value it, not because a sovereign above them will punish defection.
Three consequences follow, in the realist reading, and each matters for firms.
The first is self-help. Because no one else guarantees a state’s survival, each state must ultimately provide for its own security. It may ally with others, but alliances are arrangements of convenience, and a state that relies entirely on an ally has placed its survival in someone else’s hands.
The second is uncertainty about intentions. A state can observe another’s capabilities — its army, its industry, its population — but it cannot observe its intentions with confidence, and intentions can change faster than capabilities. A peaceful neighbour with a large army is a neighbour whose government could change. Because the cost of misjudging a hostile state is so high, states tend to plan for capabilities rather than for stated intentions.
The third is concern for relative gains. Because today’s partner may be tomorrow’s adversary, states care not only about how much they gain from cooperation, but about how much more the other side gains. A trade agreement that makes both countries richer but makes the rival richer faster shifts the balance of capabilities, and in an anarchic system that shift can be a threat.

Relative gains — the concern of a state with its gains from cooperation relative to those of its partner, rather than only with its own absolute gains, arising from the possibility that the partner’s gains will be converted into capabilities used against it (Grieco 1988).

Joseph Grieco’s 1988 article made this the central point of difference between realists and liberal institutionalists such as Keohane (Chapter 2): institutions can solve the problem of cheating, Grieco argued, but they cannot solve the problem that cooperation may help a rival more than oneself. Powell (1991) sharpened the argument by showing that the weight a state places on relative gains is not fixed but depends on circumstances — in particular, on whether the use of force is a live possibility between the two states. Where force is unthinkable, as between Canada and the United States, relative gains matter little and cooperation is easy; where it is conceivable, relative gains matter a great deal.
That is why the concept belongs in a book on international business. Relative-gains thinking is the logic by which trade becomes a security question. A sale of advanced semiconductors to a rival, or of the equipment to make them, may be profitable for the seller and beneficial for the buyer, and still be prohibited, because it narrows a capability gap the seller’s government wishes to preserve. Export controls on advanced chips are not a failure of economic reasoning; they are the application of a different calculus, in which the question is not “are we better off?” but “are we better off relative to them?”. A firm that sells into the gap between two powers’ capabilities should expect its business to be judged by the second question.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.3 Two realisms
text:
3.3 Two realisms
Realists agree that anarchy shapes behaviour. They disagree about how much power states want, and the disagreement has direct implications for what to expect from the relationship between the United States and China.

3.3.1 Defensive realism: enough is enough
Kenneth Waltz’s Theory of International Politics (1979) is the founding text of structural, or neo-, realism. Its claim is that the behaviour of states is shaped less by their domestic characteristics — their regimes, their leaders, their ideologies — than by the structure of the system they inhabit: anarchy, plus the distribution of capabilities among the units (Waltz 1979). States are alike in their basic function, which is to survive, and they differ in how well equipped they are to do it.

Balance of power — the distribution of capabilities among the major states of a system, and the tendency, in realist theory, of states to respond to a concentration of power by building their own capabilities or forming coalitions against the stronger state (“balancing”).

In Waltz’s version, states seek an appropriate amount of power: enough to be secure. Seeking more is usually self-defeating, because a state that grows too strong provokes others to balance against it, and ends up less secure than before. The system therefore tends towards equilibrium. Waltz also argued that a bipolar system — two great powers, as in the Cold War — is more stable than a multipolar one, because with only two principal actors there are fewer relationships to manage, fewer opportunities for miscalculation, and no uncertainty about who the main threat is.
Waltz’s theory sits on an older idea that is essential for understanding how conflict can arise without anyone wanting it.

Security dilemma — the situation in which measures a state takes to increase its own security, such as arming or forming alliances, reduce the security of others, who respond in kind, leaving all less secure than before even though none intended aggression (Herz 1950; Jervis 1978).

John Herz named the dilemma in 1950. Robert Jervis’s 1978 article gave it its modern form by asking when it is most severe. His answer turned on two variables: whether offensive and defensive weapons and postures can be distinguished, and whether offence or defence has the advantage. Where defensive preparations look defensive and defence is strong, states can secure themselves without threatening others, and the dilemma is mild. Where they cannot be told apart and offence is favoured, every precaution looks like preparation for attack, and the dilemma is acute.
The security dilemma is the most useful single idea in this chapter for a risk analyst, because it describes escalation without intent. A government imposes an export control to protect a technological lead; the other side reads it as an attempt at containment and responds with restrictions on a critical mineral; the first reads that as coercion and tightens the control. Each step is defensive in the mind of the state that takes it. A firm caught in the sequence does not need either government to want a confrontation in order to lose a market or a supplier.


3.3.2 Offensive realism: as much as possible
John Mearsheimer’s The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001) accepts Waltz’s starting point but reaches a darker conclusion. It rests on five bedrock assumptions (Mearsheimer 2001):

The international system is anarchic.
Great powers inherently possess some offensive military capability.
States can never be certain about other states’ intentions.
Survival is the primary goal of great powers.
Great powers are rational actors.

None of these, Mearsheimer notes, is individually alarming. Together they imply that great powers fear one another, cannot rely on anyone else for their security, and conclude that the best guarantee of survival is to be as powerful as possible relative to potential rivals. States are therefore not satisfied with an appropriate amount of power. They maximise relative power, and the ultimate goal is hegemony.
Global hegemony, however, is practically impossible, because of what Mearsheimer calls “the stopping power of water”: large bodies of water make it extremely difficult to project land power across oceans. The realistic goal is therefore regional hegemony — domination of one’s own region — together with preventing any other great power from dominating its region. The United States, on this account, is the only regional hegemon in modern history, having achieved dominance in the Western Hemisphere in the nineteenth century, and its foreign policy in the twentieth century can be read as a series of efforts to prevent the emergence of a hegemon in Europe or in North-East Asia.
The prediction for China follows mechanically. If China continues to grow economically, it will seek to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, and the United States, which has spent a century preventing exactly that, will try to stop it. Mearsheimer’s answer to the question of whether China can rise peacefully is no: the result will be intense security competition, with a considerable possibility of war.









Defensive realism (Waltz)
Offensive realism (Mearsheimer)

What restrains them?

A caution belongs here. Realism predicts competition, not war. In Waltz’s version it often predicts restraint, since overexpansion provokes balancing. Even Mearsheimer’s version predicts security competition, of which war is one possible outcome among several. A risk analyst who reads realism as a forecast of war has misread it; one who reads it as a forecast that the economic relationship will be subordinated to the strategic one has read it correctly.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.4 Power transition and the Thucydides’s Trap
text:
3.4 Power transition and the Thucydides’s Trap
Balance-of-power theory treats an equal distribution of capabilities as the condition of stability. A different tradition reverses the claim.

Power transition theory — the theory, due to A. F. K. Organski, that peace is most secure when a dominant power holds a clear preponderance and that war is most likely when a dissatisfied challenger approaches parity with it (Organski 1958; Organski and Kugler 1980).

Organski’s World Politics (1958) described the international system as a hierarchy rather than a balance. At the top sits a dominant power that built the existing international order and benefits from it; below are great powers, some satisfied with the order and some not. Industrialisation drives the rise of new powers, and their growth is uneven. Danger arises when a challenger that is dissatisfied with the order — that did not write its rules and does not benefit from them as much as it believes it should — draws close to the dominant power in capabilities. At that point the challenger has both the motive and, increasingly, the means to revise the order, and the dominant power has reason to act before its lead disappears. In empirical work, parity is often operationalised as the challenger reaching around 80 per cent of the dominant power’s capabilities. On the standard capability index discussed below, China crossed that threshold relative to the United States in 1975, two decades before it passed it — which says as much about the index as about the transition.
Organski and Kugler (1980) took the theory to data in The War Ledger, and a substantial literature followed, including the essays collected in Kugler and Lemke (1996). The tradition connects to Robert Gilpin’s account of hegemonic war, in which the order established by a dominant power becomes misaligned with the underlying distribution of power as others grow, until a war redistributes both (Gilpin 1981). It connects too to Paul Kennedy’s history of the great powers, which argued that dominant powers tend to overextend their commitments relative to their economic base (Kennedy 1987).
Power transition theory has an obvious affinity with Chapter 2. There, the question was whether the rules of the economic order would survive the shrinking share of their authors. Here, the theory supplies a mechanism: a rising power that did not write the rules is likely to be dissatisfied with them, and as its capabilities approach those of the rule-writer, its ability to revise them grows.

3.4.1 Allison’s sixteen cases
Graham Allison’s Destined for War (2017) brought the argument to a mass audience under a classical name. Thucydides, the historian of the war between Athens and Sparta in the fifth century BCE, wrote, in the translation Allison uses, that “it was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable” (Allison 2017).

From the archive · Thucydides, fifth century BCE
The Peloponnesian War began in 431 BCE and ended, after a long truce and its collapse, with the defeat of Athens in 404. Its historian, Thucydides, was an Athenian general who had been exiled after failing to prevent the loss of a city to Sparta’s forces, and who spent his exile collecting the accounts of both sides.
The sentence Allison made famous comes early in the history, where Thucydides distinguishes the immediate grievances that both sides publicly cited — disputes over Corcyra and Potidaea, over alliances and trade — from what he calls the truest cause, the one least spoken of: the growth of Athenian power and the alarm it caused in Sparta. That distinction between the stated occasion and the structural cause is the analytical move every realist since has borrowed.
It is worth reading what Thucydides does not say. He does not say that rising powers always fight ruling ones; he says this war had this cause. He was writing about a particular conflict between two particular cities, one a maritime and commercial empire and the other a land power with a very different political system. The generalisation to a law of history is Allison’s, and the critics’ first objection is to the generalisation, not to Thucydides.

Allison and the Thucydides’s Trap project at Harvard identify sixteen cases in the past five hundred years in which a rising power challenged a ruling one. Twelve ended in war. The four that did not — among them the United States overtaking Britain in the early twentieth century, and the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union — are presented as evidence that war is not inevitable, but that avoiding it requires deliberate and painful adjustment by both sides.

From the archive · Britain and the United States, 1895–1903
At the end of the nineteenth century the United States overtook Britain as the world’s largest economy, and its navy was growing. The two powers had serious quarrels. In 1895 a boundary dispute between Venezuela and British Guiana brought a sharply worded American demand that Britain accept arbitration, and talk of war on both sides of the Atlantic. Britain accepted arbitration, and a tribunal issued its award in 1899. In 1901 the Hay–Pauncefote Treaty released the United States from an earlier agreement to share control of any canal across Central America, clearing the way for an American-controlled canal at Panama. In 1903 a tribunal settled the boundary between Alaska and Canada largely in the American favour, with the British member siding with the Americans against the Canadian members’ objections.
In each dispute, the ruling power gave way. Britain, facing a rising Germany closer to home and overstretched across its empire, chose to accommodate the rising power in the Western Hemisphere rather than contest it. The case is the strongest evidence that a transition can be peaceful. It is also a reminder of the price: the accommodation was made, in part, at the expense of a third party — Canada — whose interests the ruling power judged less important than the relationship with the rising one.
For a firm, the analogy is uncomfortable and useful. A peaceful transition between great powers is not costless for everyone else. The terms on which it is reached may be paid by actors who were not at the table.



3.4.2 The critics
The Thucydides’s Trap has been criticised on four grounds.
Case selection. The cases were assembled with knowledge of the outcome. What counts as a “rising” power, a “ruling” power, and a “challenge” is elastic enough that peaceful transitions — which leave less of a trace in history than wars — may be under-counted, inflating the proportion that ended in war. A ratio of twelve to sixteen is only as informative as the rule that produced the sixteen.
Nuclear weapons. No pre-1945 case involved two powers each capable of destroying the other. Nuclear deterrence changes the expected cost of great-power war so drastically that it is not clear any pre-nuclear case is informative about the present. The Cold War, the one transition-like rivalry between nuclear powers in the dataset, did not end in war between the principals.
Interdependence. The United States and China are bound by trade, investment and finance far more tightly than Athens and Sparta were. Liberal theory holds that interdependence raises the cost of conflict and so makes it less likely. The realist reply is that Britain and Germany were also major trading partners in 1914, and fought anyway; Copeland (2015) argues that what matters is not the level of trade but leaders’ expectations of its future, so that interdependence restrains only as long as it is expected to last. Chapter 4 takes up the debate with data.
Measuring “rise”. The trap depends on knowing when a challenger is approaching parity, and that depends on how power is measured. Beckley (2018) argues that the conventional gross indicators — GDP, population, composite indices of capability — systematically overstate the power of large, populous countries, because they ignore the costs a state bears in governing, feeding, policing and protecting its population. A country with a large GDP and a large population may have much less surplus available for projecting power than the gross figures imply. Beckley proposes measures that account for such costs, and on them the gap between the United States and China looks larger and the transition further off.
The last criticism can be examined directly, because it turns on the choice of measure.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.5 Measuring power
text:
3.5 Measuring power
Every theory in this chapter turns on a quantity — the distribution of capabilities, parity, relative power — that none of them can observe directly. Power is a latent concept. What can be observed are its supposed ingredients: people, money, industry, arms. The standard way of combining them in quantitative international relations was devised in the 1960s at the University of Michigan by J. David Singer and his collaborators on the Correlates of War project.

Composite Index of National Capability (CINC) — a yearly index of a state’s material capabilities, equal to the unweighted average of its shares of the state-system total on six indicators: total population, urban population, iron and steel production, primary energy consumption, military personnel and military expenditure (Singer, Bremer, and Stuckey 1972).

The construction has three steps. For every state in the international system in a given year, take six indicators, grouped into three dimensions: demographic (total population, urban population), industrial (iron and steel production, primary energy consumption) and military (military personnel, military expenditure). For each indicator, compute the state’s share of the system total that year. Average the six shares. The result is a number between 0 and 1; summed over all states, it comes to about 1 — not exactly, because a state with a missing component is averaged over the components it has. In the current release, the National Material Capabilities dataset version 7.0, the coverage runs from 1816 to 2022, one row per state-year.
The design has real virtues. It is transparent. It is long: two centuries of comparable data, which is what allows Organski’s and Mearsheimer’s arguments to be confronted with evidence at all. And by using shares of the system total, it sidesteps the problem of comparing military spending in nineteenth-century pounds with twenty-first-century dollars — each year is compared only with itself. Mearsheimer’s own measures of latent power in the Tragedy rely on similar industrial ingredients for the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

3.5.1 What it rewards
The design also embodies a theory of power, and it is a theory of the 1960s. Two of the six components are population and two are heavy industry. CINC therefore rewards size and smokestacks. A large, populous, industrialising country — one that produces a great deal of steel and burns a great deal of energy — will score highly even if its technology is behind, its productivity low and its military poorly equipped.
The consequence is visible in the data. In version 7.0 of the National Material Capabilities dataset, China’s CINC first exceeds that of the United States in 1995; the order reverses for a single year in 2002, and China has led in every year since 2003. Other measures tell a different story. At purchasing-power parity, China’s GDP passed that of the United States in 2014, according to the World Bank’s data; at market exchange rates it never has. On military expenditure the gap is wider still: about a quarter of the American figure in 2022 in the Correlates of War series, about a third in 2025 in the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s (SIPRI) database, whose Chinese figures are its own estimates. One underlying reality, four answers: 1995, 2014, not yet, and not close.






Figure 3.1: China relative to the United States: past parity on the capability index since 1995 and at purchasing-power parity since 2014, but at 63 per cent of US GDP at market exchange rates and 36 per cent of US military spending in 2025. Source: COW NMC v7.0; World Bank WDI; SIPRI (constant 2024 US dollars).



Figure 3.1 puts the four series on one scale, with lines at parity and at the 80 per cent threshold, and Table 3.1 dates the crossings. The measures disagree not only about the level but about the shape of the transition. On the capability index China was already at 79 per cent of the United States in 1990, before its take-off showed in any output statistic, and entered the danger zone in 1975, in the last years of the Cultural Revolution. At purchasing-power parity it stood at 19 per cent in 1990 and reached parity in 2014. At market exchange rates it rose from 6 per cent to 77 and fell back as the renminbi weakened and American nominal growth outpaced China’s. On military money it went from under 3 per cent to just over a third. Four histories: a transition long completed, one recently completed, one stalled, one not begun.

The measures sort themselves by what they weigh. The two that put China ahead count physical volumes — tonnes of steel, the domestic price of a haircut; the two that put the United States ahead count things priced in world markets. Purchasing-power parity is the better guide to what a government can buy at home; market exchange rates to what it can buy abroad, and to the market a foreign firm earns revenue in. A multinational that reports its Chinese sales in dollars lives in the market-exchange-rate world, whatever the capability index says.
The size bias is visible even earlier in the series. In the 1860s, 1870s and most of the 1880s — decades in which China was losing wars to European powers and ceding territory and treaty ports — its CINC exceeded that of the United States, because its population was vastly larger and American industry had not yet grown to its later scale. No historian of the period would call Qing China the more powerful of the two. The index does, for a quarter of a century, and for the same reason that it dates the modern transition early.
Because the index is a simple average, the size bias can be taken apart component by component (Figure 3.2). In 2022 China produced 54 per cent of the system’s recorded iron and steel and consumed 30 per cent of its primary energy, against 4 and 14 per cent for the United States; it held 18 per cent of world and of urban population, against about 4 and 3. Only on military expenditure does the United States lead — 42 per cent against 11.






Figure 3.2: China’s capability lead in 2022 rests on iron and steel (54 per cent of the system total against 4 per cent for the United States), energy and population; the United States leads only on military expenditure (42 per cent against 11). Source: Correlates of War, National Material Capabilities v7.0.



Steel alone contributes nine of China’s 23 points. Without it, China still leads on the other five components, by 17 points to 14; on the two military components alone the order reverses, 10 against 24. In 1995, the crossover year, the two countries each produced about 13 per cent of the system’s steel, and nearly all of China’s subsequent gain came from the steel and energy columns — the construction boom of the 2000s and 2010s and the coal-fired power that drove it. That capacity could in principle be turned to shipbuilding and munitions. But a measure of national power whose largest driver is a sector Chinese policy has spent a decade trying to shrink needs careful reading.


3.5.2 What it misses
CINC is equally instructive for what it cannot see. It has no component for technology — the quality of weapons, the sophistication of industry, the capacity to innovate. It has no component for alliances, although a state with many capable allies commands far more power than its own figures suggest. It has nothing on financial power: the role of a state’s currency in international payments, the depth of its capital markets, its control of the institutions through which money moves. And it has nothing on control of networks — the payment systems, cloud platforms and communications infrastructure that Farrell and Newman (2019) identify as instruments of coercion (Chapter 2). These are precisely the forms of power that reach firms most directly, and Chapters 8, 10 and 11 return to them.
The choice of measure is not a technicality, as Beckley’s critique shows: on gross resources China caught up long ago; on net resources, quality-weighted military capability or control of networks, the picture changes. Each measure is defensible. None is neutral.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.6 Reading two centuries in one chart
text:
3.6 Reading two centuries in one chart
The long-run chart of capability shares is a compressed history of the modern state system, and reading it well requires knowing where its seams are, so that the anomalies are recognisable as anomalies.
The first seam is that the chart is not a chart of a fixed set of countries. The Correlates of War data describe the members of the state system in each year — some 17,000 state-years in the current release — and membership changes. China and Japan enter the data in 1860. Germany, coded GMY, disappears in 1945 and returns in 1991; in between, the Federal Republic and the Democratic Republic appear as separate states, GFR and GDR. Japan is absent from 1946 to 1951, under occupation. The Soviet Union, by contrast, is coded as RUS throughout, so that Russia, the USSR and Russia again form one continuous series. Each produces a break or a continuity that has nothing to do with power and everything to do with coding. The codes themselves look like ISO codes and are not — the United Kingdom is UKG, France FRN — so that any combination with the World Bank data of Chapter 2 has to be made through a concordance rather than by matching letters.
The second seam is arithmetic. Missing values of the six components are coded as -9, not left blank, and the index is averaged over whatever components a state has. Summed over all states, CINC should equal one; in practice the yearly total runs from 1.000 to about 1.075, highest in 1860 and generally above one in the nineteenth century, when the components are most often missing.
The third seam is the joining of sources over time. Between 2016 and 2017 the urban population recorded for the United States falls from about 198 million to about 110 million, while its total population continues to rise; the American share of the world’s urban population, as the dataset counts it, drops from about 8 per cent to about 3 per cent in a single year. No migration explains that. It is a change in source or definition, and because urban population is one of six components, it removes nearly a tenth of the United States’ CINC score — from 0.133 to 0.122 — overnight. China’s urban population jumps in the same year in the opposite direction. A reader who saw the gap between the two powers widen in 2017 would be reading a revision, not a shift in power.
The fourth thing is the substantive story, and read with these cautions it is clear (Figure 3.3). Britain holds the largest share from 1816 until the 1890s — a third of the system’s capabilities at the start of the series, and still more than a quarter in 1860; the United States passes it briefly in 1892 and for good in 1897, in the years when, as the archive above recounts, Britain chose to accommodate it. The two World Wars violently rearrange the distribution: the American share spikes to 38 per cent in 1919, as wartime spending is counted against a devastated Europe, and peaks in 1945 at 38.4 per cent of the system’s capabilities, the highest any state reaches in two centuries. The Cold War appears as Waltz’s bipolarity made visible — two powers far above the rest — and on this index the Soviet Union actually leads from 1971 to 1988, a reminder of how much weight the measure gives to steel, energy and soldiers and how little to technology. From the 1990s, China’s share rises past both, to about 23 per cent in 2022 against about 12 per cent for the United States.






Figure 3.3: Britain leads until the 1890s, the United States from 1897 (peaking at 38 per cent in 1945), the Soviet Union on this index from 1971 to 1988, and China since 1995. Source: Correlates of War, National Material Capabilities v7.0.



Two features of the chart deserve more attention. The first is the shape of American dominance: the 1945 peak reflects the destruction of every other industrial power, and it decays fast — 28 per cent in 1950, 14 per cent by 1990. A present-day share of 12 per cent is not a collapse; what changed after 1990 was which line sat above the American one. The second is that for the period in which most Western managers formed their picture of the world, the index shows a Soviet Union at or above the United States — wrong for the reason the Chinese figures need caution today: the index counts inputs, not how efficiently they are used. The Soviet line falls from about 18 per cent in 1985 to under 7 in 1992, partly because post-1991 Russia is a smaller state than the Soviet Union it continues in the data.

3.6.1 Bipolar, multipolar, or something else?
The chart also bears on a question that has occupied realists since the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991: what is the polarity of the system now? The 1990s were widely described as a unipolar moment, with the United States unmatched. Waltz expected that unipolarity would not last, because other states would balance against a power with no counterweight. Whether the present system is returning to bipolarity — the United States and China — or moving to a multipolar one with several significant powers is contested, and the answer depends, once again, on the measure.
Polarity has its own measurement tradition: Ray and Singer (1973) proposed an index of the concentration of capabilities among the major powers. A simpler reading takes the shares of the three largest states each year. A system is bipolar when the gap between the second and the third is wide, multipolar when it is narrow.






Figure 3.4: On the capability index, the gap between the second- and third-largest states, wide in the Cold War and after 1991, had narrowed to about two and a half points by 2022. Source: Correlates of War, National Material Capabilities v7.0.



In 1950 the largest state held 28 per cent of the system’s capabilities, the second 18 and the third 12 (Figure 3.4). The gap was wider still in the mid-1990s, but the index names the top two in 1995 as the United States and China, at 14.3 and 14.1 per cent. On CINC there was no “unipolar moment” — the opposite of the reading of Wohlforth (1999), who argued that the post-Cold War system was unipolar and, because unipolar, durable, on measures that weight quality: defence spending, research and development, output at market prices.
By 2022 the band has narrowed to about two and a half points: China 23 per cent, the United States 12, India nearly 10. India’s share reached 80 per cent of the American one in 2017 — the year of the American urban-population revision — and stood there in 2022. A mechanical reader would say the United States is “approaching parity” from below with India, whose military spending in 2025 was about a tenth of the American figure. Yet India’s population, steel and energy are large and growing; if latent power is what they measure, the data point to a three-cornered distribution.
The debate over the present configuration is a debate about weights. Brooks and Wohlforth (2016) argued that technology-intensive military power makes it harder for a rising state to convert economic size into superpower capabilities, and treated China as, at most, an emerging potential superpower. Others see a return to bipolarity, or a world of several centres. Each answer is a choice of yardstick.
Nor is balancing always military. Pape (2005) argued that states facing an American lead too large to balance by arms would turn to soft balancing — denying territory, entangling diplomacy in institutions, economic strengthening — to raise the costs of American action. Its instruments are commercial, which makes it the form that reaches firms: the refused port call becomes a refused licence, and the coalition becomes a payment system built to work around the dominant power’s.
The question matters to firms because the two configurations imply different environments. A bipolar system tends to produce two blocs with clear membership, so that the firm’s problem is being made to choose a side. A multipolar system produces more hedging states — governments that trade with both sides and bargain between them — and therefore more room for firms to locate operations in third countries open to both. The geography of “connector” economies, which Chapter 4 examines with trade data, is a direct consequence of which of the two worlds firms are in.


3.6.2 The military money
If the capability index flatters size, military expenditure flatters quality, and it is the measure on which the unipolar reading rests. Figure 3.5 divides each country’s spending in the SIPRI database, in constant 2024 dollars, by the world total, which SIPRI reports from 1988.






Figure 3.5: The American share of world military spending fell from 53 per cent in 2010 to 34 per cent in 2025; China’s rose to 12 per cent and Russia’s recovered to 6. Source: SIPRI Military Expenditure Database, 2026 release, constant 2024 US dollars.



The United States spent 47 per cent of the world’s military budget in 1988 and 53 per cent at the peak in 2010, during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Its share fell to 34 per cent in 2025, as much through others’ growth as through restraint: world spending rose from about 1,961 billion dollars in 2015 to 2,771 billion in 2025, in constant 2024 prices, while American spending fell in 2025 from 1,005 to 929 billion. China’s rise has been steady rather than spectacular — from 196 to 335 billion dollars over the decade, 12 per cent of the world total. The United States still spent 2.8 times as much.

Table 3.2 is a portrait of a system rearming. Russia’s spending more than doubled in a decade and Ukraine’s rose sixteen-fold; Germany’s more than doubled; Japan’s rose by 60 per cent. Each increase is defensive in the mind of the state that makes it, and read by others as a reason for their own — the security dilemma in a table.
Spending has its own measurement problems. Market exchange rates understate what a lower-cost economy buys, since Chinese soldiers and shipyard workers are paid less than American ones; purchasing-power parity raises China’s figure but overstates what it can buy of weapons priced in world markets. China’s official budget excludes items SIPRI adds back, which is why SIPRI’s figure is higher and marked as an estimate. And much of the American budget goes on personnel, health care and global bases that a power concentrating on its own region does not need.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.7 How a firm would know the balance is shifting
text:
3.7 How a firm would know the balance is shifting
The second half of the chapter’s question — how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting? — has two answers, a structural one and a behavioural one.
The structural answer is the one the data above supply: track the distribution of capabilities on several measures, and watch the ratios. A challenger’s share approaching the dominant power’s on one measure, while still far behind on others, is a transition in progress and a transition contested; it is the situation in which the security dilemma is most acute, because each side can read the evidence as it wishes. Structural indicators of this kind, in the typology of Chapter 1, explain why tension is building. They do not say when it will matter.
The behavioural answer is to watch what states do with the rules. A shifting balance shows up first not in war but in the instruments of economic statecraft: export controls, investment screening, sanctions and counter-sanctions, restrictions on data, rules about where a firm may source a component. These are the measures by which states convert relative-gains concerns into policy, and they are observable — in official gazettes, in company disclosures, in the event datasets of later chapters — long before any military confrontation. For a firm, the most reliable signal that the balance is shifting is a change in which rules it is being asked to follow.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.8 What it means for the multinational
text:
3.8 What it means for the multinational
The realist frame leads to three implications for a firm, each of which recurs later in the book.
The balance of power sets the rules of trade. Who can impose sanctions, export controls and market-access conditions depends on who holds capabilities others need: the largest market, the dominant currency, the critical technology. A firm’s exposure to a state’s economic statecraft is a function of how much of its business depends on capabilities that state controls.
A transition changes which rules a firm follows. A firm operating in both the United States and China increasingly faces two compliance regimes — and, since China adopted its own instruments of counter-sanction in 2020 and 2021, the possibility of penalties in one jurisdiction for complying with the other’s rules. The question “is this transaction legal?” has acquired a second clause: “legal where, and under whose law?”.
Relative gains turn commerce into security. Products that would make a rival stronger — advanced semiconductors, the tools that make them, artificial intelligence, batteries, aerospace — move from the trade ministry’s jurisdiction to the security establishment’s. For firms in these sectors, market access is no longer negotiated mainly on economic grounds, and commercial arguments about mutual benefit carry less weight than they did.
Mapped onto the five channels of this book, the balance of power runs through every one, but most directly through market access (which markets will remain open to firms from which bloc) and assets and people (where conflict, if it comes, will fall). It reaches inputs through export controls on critical goods, finance and payments through the dominant currency, and data and operations through the control of networks.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.9 A short review of the literature
text:
3.9 A short review of the literature

Realism’s modern structural form begins with Waltz (1979), who explained state behaviour by anarchy and the distribution of capabilities and judged bipolarity the more stable configuration. The security dilemma that underlies much of it was named by Herz (1950) and given its analytical form by Jervis (1978), who related its severity to the offence–defence balance. Grieco (1988) made relative gains the realist objection to liberal institutionalism, and Powell (1991) showed that the weight states put on relative gains depends on whether force is a live option between them. Mearsheimer (2001) pushed the structural argument to its offensive conclusion — power maximisation and regional hegemony — and applied it to China.
A parallel tradition locates danger in hierarchy rather than balance. Organski (1958) introduced power transition theory; Organski and Kugler (1980) and the contributions in Kugler and Lemke (1996) tested it on data. Gilpin (1981) gave a systemic account of hegemonic war, and Kennedy (1987) a historical account of how great powers rise and decline relative to their economic base. Allison (2017) reframed the transition debate for the US–China relationship through sixteen historical cases.
Measurement runs through all of it. Singer, Bremer, and Stuckey (1972) introduced the Composite Index of National Capability and the Correlates of War data on which much of the quantitative literature rests. Beckley (2018) argued that gross indicators overstate the power of populous states and proposed net measures, which change the dating of the US–China transition. Farrell and Newman (2019) identified a form of power — control over network hubs — that no capability index was designed to capture.
The through-line is that every theory of the balance of power is also a claim about how to measure it, and that the measurement is where theories can be checked against the world — and where they most often disagree.

title: 3  Anarchy and the Balance of Power: Who Sets the Terms When No One Governs
section: 3.10 Which kind of power the firm depends on
text:
3.10 Which kind of power the firm depends on
Realism begins from an absence. There is no government above states, and so the rules on which firms rely — the open market, the convertible currency, the procedure for settling a dispute — are kept only as long as the states that hold the relevant capabilities find it in their interest to keep them. That is not a prediction of war. Defensive realists expect restraint; offensive realists expect security competition; power transition theorists expect danger only where a dissatisfied challenger nears parity. What all three share is the claim that the economic relationship between great powers is, in the end, subordinate to the strategic one. Export controls, investment screens and counter-sanctions are what that subordination looks like before anyone fires a shot.
The evidence of this chapter adds a second claim, about measurement. Every theory of the balance of power turns on a quantity — capabilities, parity, relative power — that cannot be observed directly, and the answer to the question “has the transition happened?” depends on how the quantity is built. On an index that rewards population and heavy industry, China overtook the United States in 1995, and Qing China was ahead of it in the 1870s. On output at purchasing-power parity it did so in 2014; at market exchange rates it has not; on military spending it is far behind. Each number is correctly computed; none is the balance of power. A board slide that says “China has overtaken the United States” without saying on what has said nothing a decision can use.
For a multinational, the useful question is therefore not which measure is right in general, but which kind of power its own exposures depend on. A firm whose risk lies in market access needs to know who holds the largest market and the willingness to close it. A firm whose risk lies in inputs needs to know who controls the technology, the mineral or the equipment that cannot be replaced quickly. A firm whose risk lies in finance needs to know whose currency clears its payments, and a firm whose risk lies in data needs to know whose networks its operations run through. On some of these dimensions the transition is far advanced; on others it has barely begun; on the forms of power that reach firms most directly — currency, networks, critical technology — the standard capability index does not look at all.
A crossover on a capability chart, then, does not tell a multinational that war is coming — power transition theory makes war likelier near parity only if the challenger is dissatisfied, and dissatisfaction is not on the chart. Nor does it say that the firm’s Chinese revenue is at risk or its American suppliers safe. It says that, on one measure built in the 1960s around steel, energy and soldiers, and ending in 2022, the distribution of material capabilities has shifted. Whether that shift reaches the firm depends on whether the measure can see the kind of power the firm actually depends on — and, as the chapters on trade, sanctions, cyber operations and space will show, the kinds that matter most are often the ones it cannot.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation: From Commercial Peace to Rival Blocs
text:
4.1 An old promise, and an old embarrassment
The idea that commerce keeps the peace is older than the discipline that now tests it. Montesquieu put it in a sentence in 1748 — peace is the natural effect of trade — and the sentence did a great deal of work for the next century and a half. Richard Cobden built a political career on it: the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 and the Anglo-French commercial treaty of 1860 that carries his name were sold, in part, as instruments of peace between nations that had spent much of the previous century fighting each other. The argument was not that merchants are nicer than generals. It was that exchange creates gains, that war destroys them, and that a state which stands to lose a great deal from fighting will think harder before it fights.
The argument’s most famous restatement came at the worst possible moment.
This chapter takes the argument seriously, sets out the realist reply, asks what a century of evidence has settled, and then turns to the question that has replaced it. The old question was whether trade pacifies. The question that matters to a multinational in the 2020s is different: if states have begun to trade more with friends than with rivals, how does a firm find out which side each of its markets is on, and how fast the lines are hardening? That question has an empirical answer, assembled from public data, and the second half of the chapter shows how the answer is built and how far it can be trusted.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation: From Commercial Peace to Rival Blocs
text:
From the archive · Angell, 1910
In 1910 Norman Angell, a British journalist, published The Great Illusion (Angell 1910). Its claim is usually remembered as “war has become impossible”, which is not what it said. Angell’s claim was narrower and more interesting: that in an economy of credit, contracts and cross-border investment, conquest no longer pays. A victor cannot seize the wealth of an industrial country, because that wealth consists of claims, trading relationships and productive organisation that collapse when they are seized. The economic case for war, he argued, rested on an illusion — the belief that national wealth is a stock of things that can be carried off.
The book sold in enormous numbers and was translated widely. Four years later Britain and Germany — two of each other’s most important trading partners, bound by finance, shipping and insurance as well as by goods — were at war. The war went on for more than four years and destroyed exactly the wealth Angell said it would destroy.
The episode is usually told as a refutation. It is better read as a lesson about which claim was refuted. Angell was largely right that the war would be ruinous for the victors as well as the vanquished. What failed was the inference from war does not pay to states will therefore not make war. Leaders in 1914 were not computing the net present value of conflict, or were computing it with expectations about the war’s length and cost that turned out to be badly wrong. Angell received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1933, as the next European war was being prepared. The commercial peace has lived with the embarrassment of 1914 ever since, and every serious version of the argument is a version that tries to explain it.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation: From Commercial Peace to Rival Blocs
section: 4.2 Four reasons trade might pacify
text:
4.2 Four reasons trade might pacify
The modern version of the argument is less a single claim than a family of mechanisms, and they are worth keeping apart because they fail in different ways.

Commercial peace — the proposition that economic interdependence between two states lowers the probability that they will come into militarised conflict with each other. It is a claim about dyads — pairs of states — and it is probabilistic: it predicts fewer disputes, not none.

The first mechanism is opportunity cost. Conflict disrupts trade, and the more a dyad trades, the more it stands to lose. This is Angell’s mechanism with the conquest argument stripped out, and it was formalised by Polachek (1980), who modelled conflict as an activity whose price rises with the gains from trade that it puts at risk. Its weakness is the weakness of 1914: it assumes leaders weigh those costs, and weigh them accurately.
The second is signalling. Interdependent states have a menu of costly actions short of force — threatening, restricting or suspending economic ties — that allow them to reveal how much they care about an issue. A state that is willing to lose trade to make a point is telling its rival something credible about its resolve, and credible information reduces the risk of miscalculation that rationalist accounts of war identify as its main cause. On this account trade matters not because it makes war expensive but because it makes communication possible.
The third is domestic coalitions. Trade creates exporters, importers, port operators, banks and their employees, all of whom have something to lose from a rupture with the partner. They lobby. A government contemplating confrontation faces an organised constituency on the other side, and the larger the trade, the larger the constituency. This mechanism is the one most familiar to a multinational, because the multinational is frequently the constituency.
The fourth is institutions. Trade agreements create committees, forums and dispute-settlement procedures through which grievances can be processed before they escalate, and they create repeated interaction among officials who come to know each other. Mansfield and Pevehouse (2000) found that pairs of states belonging to the same preferential trading arrangement are less prone to militarised disputes, and that the effect strengthens as trade between them grows — a result that has made institutions the most robust strand of the liberal argument.
Statistical work on dyads from the 1990s onwards gave these mechanisms empirical weight. Oneal and Russett (1997), using dyads from 1950 to 1985, titled their findings with some confidence — the classical liberals were right — and the programme culminated in Russett and Oneal (2001), which set interdependence alongside democracy and shared membership of international organisations as the three legs of a “Kantian” peace. Dyads that trade more relative to their GDP experience fewer militarised disputes. That correlation is real. What it means is a different question.

title: 4  Trade, Conflict and Geoeconomic Fragmentation: From Commercial Peace to Rival Blocs
section: 4.3 The realist reply: interdependence as exposure
text:
4.3 The realist reply: interdependence as exposure
The realist critique does not deny that trade creates gains. It denies that gains are what states care about most. In an anarchic system — the world described in Chapter 3, with no authority above states to enforce agreements — a state’s first concern is survival, and every economic relationship is evaluated for what it does to security.
Seen that way, interdependence is a polite word for vulnerability. If a state depends on a rival for food, fuel or critical components, the rival holds a lever over it. Kenneth Waltz drew the conclusion that great powers will try to limit such dependence, and that where they cannot, they may be tempted to secure supplies by other means (Waltz 1979). The relationship that liberals see as a bond, realists see as a hostage.
The argument has a precise early statement in economics, and it was written by someone watching it happen.
Albert Hirschman, a refugee economist writing during the Second World War, analysed how Germany in the 1930s had organised its foreign trade with the smaller states of south-eastern Europe (Hirschman 1945). The terms were often generous. Germany bought their agricultural exports in quantities no one else would, through bilateral clearing arrangements that tied payment to purchases of German goods. The result was that a large share of each small country’s trade came to depend on a single partner, while each of them was a trivial share of Germany’s. Hirschman separated two effects. The supply effect is the gain in resources that trade brings a state. The influence effect is the power a state acquires over partners for whom the relationship matters much more than it does to the state itself — because breaking it would cost them dearly and cost it little. The influence effect depends not on the volume of trade but on its asymmetry and its concentration, and to measure concentration Hirschman proposed an index that, after a later rediscovery by Herfindahl, became the standard measure of market concentration in competition policy. The intellectual ancestor of every modern dependency dashboard was designed to measure geopolitical leverage.
The index is the square root of the sum of the squared shares of each partner in a country’s exports, times a hundred: 100 if everything goes to one partner, close to zero if exports are spread evenly across many. Table 4.1 computes it from the exporter-reported goods exports in the IMF’s partner-country trade statistics (International Monetary Fund 2026).
