7.4.1 Geopolitical risk as newspaper attention
Caldara and Iacoviello define geopolitical risk as the threat, realisation and escalation of adverse events associated with wars, terrorism and tensions between states that affect the normal and peaceful course of international relations (Caldara and Iacoviello 2022). Their index counts, each month, the share of articles in a fixed set of newspapers that contain words from eight categories: war threats, peace threats, military build-ups, nuclear threats, terror threats, beginning of war, escalation of war and terror acts. The first five form a sub-index of threats, the last three a sub-index of acts. The series is rescaled so that its average over a base period equals 100, and national indices are built by requiring that the article also mention the country.
The theory of risk embedded in this procedure is explicit: geopolitical risk is what informed newspaper readers in a few large democracies are being told to worry about. The split between threats and acts is not a technical detail. It distinguishes the risk that something will happen from the fact that it has, and the two behave differently — threats can rise for months before an act, and an act can resolve uncertainty as well as create it. Any hand-coding protocol that borrows the eight categories needs a rule for the headline that reports both, and the natural rule is that acts beat threats.
The authors validate the index in two ways. Historically, the archive lets them extend the series back to 1900, and it spikes where a historian would want it to: around the two world wars, at the beginning of the Korean War, during the Cuban Missile Crisis and after 11 September 2001. Economically, higher readings foreshadow lower investment and employment and are associated with a higher probability of disaster and larger downside risks, and the adverse consequences come from threats as well as from acts. They also build industry- and firm-level versions, and find that investment falls more in industries exposed to aggregate geopolitical risk (Caldara and Iacoviello 2022). The first test is of face validity; the second, of predictive validity, is the more demanding.
The published series makes the split concrete (Figure 7.1). The two sub-indices are correlated — 0.59, month by month, since 1985 — but the episodes that dominate them are different. The attacks of 11 September 2001 were an act before they were anything else: in September 2001 the acts sub-index stood at 841, more than eight times its 1985–2019 average, while the threats sub-index stood at 260. The run-up to the invasion of Iraq was the opposite kind of episode. From December 2002 to February 2003, months of ultimatums and inspections, threats climbed from 183 to 297 while acts stayed below about 215; only in March 2003, the month of the invasion, did acts overtake threats, at 429 against 362. The war in Ukraine, too, began in the newspapers as a threat. From October 2021 to January 2022, while Russian forces massed on the border, the threats sub-index averaged 143 and the acts sub-index 53. In February 2022, the month of the invasion, threats stood at 321 and acts at 105; acts reached 251 only in March.






Figure 7.1: Threats and acts are different series: 2001 registered as acts; before the invasions of 2003 and 2022, threats rose first. Monthly sub-indices, 1985–2019 average = 100, three-month centred average. Source: Caldara and Iacoviello, Geopolitical Risk index.



Two lessons follow. The headline GPR, which combines the two, can rise for very different reasons, so a reader who sees a spike should ask which sub-index produced it. And the threats sub-index is the one with a claim to foresight: it rose in the autumn of 2021, when the decisions open to a firm — to build inventory, to move staff, to hedge a currency — could still be taken. The scale deserves a word too. “100” is the average of 1985–2019, so a reading of 146, the value for September 2026, says that the share of articles about geopolitical tension was nearly half as high again as its long-run norm. It does not say that the world was 46 per cent more dangerous.


7.4.2 Policy uncertainty as a three-way conjunction
Baker, Bloom and Davis built the Economic Policy Uncertainty index on a different logic (Baker, Bloom, and Davis 2016). An article counts only if it contains a term from each of three sets: one about the economy, one about policy and one about uncertainty. The conjunction is the clever part. A filter on “uncertainty” alone would capture weather and sport; a filter on “policy” alone would capture every legislative report. Requiring all three narrows the count to articles that discuss uncertainty about economic policy, at the cost of missing articles that discuss it without using any of the listed words.
What distinguishes the EPU work methodologically is the audit. Human readers coded a large sample of articles, and the policy term set was tuned to reduce errors in both directions against their judgements. The audit does not make the index perfect. It makes its error rates known, which is the more useful property. The global index is a GDP-weighted average of national indices, published in two versions — weighted by current-price GDP and by purchasing-power-parity GDP — and the choice between them is a small instance of the aggregation decisions discussed below: the second gives large emerging economies more weight, and therefore gives their politics more voice in what is called “global” uncertainty.
Set beside each other, the two newspaper indices tell different histories (Figure 7.2). Over the 355 months from January 1997 to July 2026 that both cover, their correlation is 0.26 in levels and 0.19 in monthly changes — positive, but low enough to say that they measure different things. Their largest episodes barely overlap. Taking the five highest months of each, at least six months apart, the geopolitical risk index peaks in October 2001, March 2003, March 2026, March 2022 and June 2025; the global policy uncertainty index in April 2025, March 2026, May 2020, November 2020 and June 2019. Only March 2026 — the war of the United States and Israel with Iran (Chapter 1) — appears in both lists. The attacks of 2001 and the invasion of Iraq barely moved economic policy uncertainty; the pandemic and the American tariff announcements of April 2025 barely moved geopolitical risk.






Figure 7.2: The two best-known newspaper indices record different crises: wars and terrorism for one; the pandemic, elections and tariffs for the other. Both rescaled to their 1997–2019 means, three-month centred average. Source: Caldara and Iacoviello; Baker, Bloom and Davis, global EPU weighted by current-price GDP.



This is what the definitions predict. A firm exposed through tariffs and export controls will find its risk in the EPU series and little of it in the GPR series, whose eight categories exclude trade conflict; a firm with plants near a contested border will find the reverse. The weighting of the global EPU index, by contrast, matters much less than the definitions: the versions weighted by current-price and by purchasing-power-parity GDP correlate at 0.997 over the same months. The choice of weights changes whose newspapers count for how much; the choice of concept changes which crises exist.


7.4.3 Political risk as what managers discuss
Hassan, Hollander, van Lent and Tahoun asked a question the newspaper indices cannot answer: how much political risk does an individual firm face, and does it matter for what the firm does (Hassan et al. 2019)? Their text is not newspapers but the transcripts of quarterly earnings conference calls, in which senior managers present results and answer questions from analysts. An earnings call is where a firm’s leadership, questioned by people paid to find weaknesses, talks about what worries it.
Their dictionary is not written by hand. It is learned. The authors took a body of political texts and a body of non-political texts and identified two-word combinations — bigrams — that are frequent in the first and rare in the second. They then counted, in each transcript, the political bigrams that appear close to a synonym of “risk” or “uncertainty”, weighted them by how distinctively political they are, and divided by the length of the transcript. The result, PRisk, is a firm-quarter measure of the share of the conversation devoted to political risk.

Dictionary method — a measurement procedure that assigns texts to categories by counting words or phrases from a pre-specified list. The list may be written by the analyst (GPR, EPU) or learned from labelled texts (PRisk). Either way it is a theory of what the concept looks like in language, and its validity depends on whether that theory holds in the texts to which it is applied.

The proximity requirement deserves a moment. Counting political bigrams alone would measure how much a firm talks about politics — which may reflect opportunity as much as risk, or simply a chief executive’s interests. Requiring that the political language appear near the language of risk and uncertainty turns a measure of political attention into a measure of political risk. It is the same logic as EPU’s three-way conjunction, applied at the level of a sentence rather than an article.
The dependence of a dictionary on its domain is not a hypothetical worry. Loughran and McDonald showed that the general-purpose word lists then in common use classified much of the ordinary vocabulary of corporate filings as negative — words such as “liability”, “tax” or “cost” that in a financial report are neutral descriptions — and built a finance-specific list in response (Loughran and McDonald 2011). Tetlock’s earlier work on newspaper pessimism and stock prices had shown that a dictionary measure of tone could carry real information about markets (Tetlock 2007). Together they make the point that runs through this chapter: a dictionary works only for the texts it was built for.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.5 What the firm-level measure found
text:
7.5 What the firm-level measure found
Hassan and colleagues validated PRisk in three ways. First, its aggregate across firms moves over time with the EPU index, as it should if both capture the same variation in political uncertainty. Second, it varies intuitively across sectors and over time. Third, and most persuasively, firms with high PRisk behave as theory predicts firms facing political risk should behave: they cut investment and hiring, and they become more active politically, lobbying more and donating more to politicians. A measure that predicted nothing about behaviour would be a curiosity. A measure that predicts the behaviour the concept implies has passed a test of validity that no amount of reliability could substitute for.
The public release of the data lets anyone see the first of these tests again. The 2022 vintage of the file contains 225,954 firm-quarters for firms headquartered in the United States — 7,073 firms between the first quarter of 2002 and the first quarter of 2022, a median of 2,932 in each quarter. Averaged across firms each quarter, and expressed in standard deviations of the firm-level measure, PRisk tracks the American EPU index closely: the correlation between the two quarterly series is 0.80 (Figure 7.3). Newspapers and earnings calls agree about when political uncertainty was high for listed American firms: at the end of 2008, in the dispute over the “fiscal cliff” at the end of 2012, and above all in the second quarter of 2020, when average PRisk reached 1.02 standard deviations, its highest in the series. They also disagree in instructive places. The confrontation over the federal debt ceiling in the summer of 2011 doubled the quarterly EPU index, from 116 to 235, but moved average PRisk only from 0.56 to 0.64 standard deviations: newspapers wrote a great deal about a crisis that most managers, on their calls, did not treat as a risk to their own business.






Figure 7.3: Political risk in earnings calls moves with newspaper-based policy uncertainty, and firms spread apart when the average rises. Quarterly mean PRisk of US-headquartered listed firms, in standard deviations, with the 10th–90th percentile range; US EPU on the right axis. Source: Hassan, Hollander, van Lent and Tahoun, firm-level political risk (2022q1 vintage); Baker, Bloom and Davis.



The finding that matters most for a multinational concerns where the variation lies. Most of the variation in political risk is not common to all firms at a given time, nor common to all firms in a sector; it is specific to the firm. Two companies in the same industry, in the same quarter, can face very different political risk, because they sell to different governments, depend on different regulations, source from different countries or hold different licences. Two further results sharpen the point. The dispersion of political risk across firms widens when aggregate political risk is high, so that the moments at which a national index rises are precisely the moments at which it says least about any one firm. And when the measure is broken down by topic, firms that talk more about the risks of a given political topic increase their lobbying on that topic, and not on others, in the following quarter (Hassan et al. 2019). Managers do not merely worry in general; they worry about something, and act on it.
The band in Figure 7.3 shows the second of those results in the public data. Its edges are the 10th and 90th percentiles of firms in each quarter, and it widens precisely when the average rises: the correlation between the quarterly average and the distance between the two percentiles is 0.95. A quarter of high political risk for the average firm is a quarter in which firms differ from each other more than usual.
How much of the variation is common and how much belongs to the firm can be measured directly, by asking how much of the variance of PRisk the quarter explains on its own, and how much more the identity of the firm adds (Figure 7.4). The quarter — everything that all American listed firms shared in a given three months, from elections to wars to pandemics — explains about 1 per cent. Permanent differences between firms, the fact that a defence contractor always talks more about politics than a maker of software, explain another 21 per cent. The remaining 78 per cent is variation within the firm from one quarter to the next that other firms did not share. The authors’ own decomposition, which uses sectors rather than individual firms, reaches the same conclusion: the common component is a small fraction of the whole (Hassan et al. 2019).






Figure 7.4: Most variation in firm-level political risk is neither common to all firms nor a permanent trait of the firm. Shares of the variance of PRisk across US firm-quarters, 2002–2022. Source: Hassan, Hollander, van Lent and Tahoun, firm-level political risk (2022q1 vintage); decomposition by the author.



Part of the residual is noise — a chief executive’s words on one call are partly accidental — so the 78 per cent is an upper bound on the firm-specific risk that matters, not an estimate of it. But the behavioural tests in the paper show that much of it is real, because noise does not make firms lobby on the very topic they talk about. Most of the political risk a firm faces is its own; the part it shares with every other firm is the smallest part.
The implication is uncomfortable for anyone who buys a country-risk score. An aggregate index measures what is common; the political risk that reaches a particular firm is mostly what is not. A board that tracks a national index and believes it is tracking its own exposure is watching the weather report for a region while the risk is in the plumbing of its own building.
This is where the five channels used throughout this book earn their place. Political risk reaches a multinational through market access (who may sell what to whom), inputs (what can be bought, and from where), finance (who will lend, insure, settle), assets and people (what can be seized, damaged or detained) and data and operations (what can be stored, transferred or shut down). A newspaper index measures, at best, the climate in which these channels operate; PRisk measures how worried a firm’s own managers are, which integrates the channels from the inside. Neither tells the firm which channel is exposed. That is the job of a composite exposure index built for a named firm, channel by channel, and the arithmetic of such indices is the subject of the second half of this chapter.

section: 7.6 Two coders and a protocol
text:
7.6 Two coders and a protocol
The obvious measure of reliability is percent agreement: the share of items on which two coders chose the same category. It is intuitive and misleading. Two coders who assigned codes at random, in proportion to how often each category occurs, would agree often. In a sample where four headlines in five are not about geopolitics at all, two coders who both write “not geopolitical” for every item will agree on most of them, while having measured nothing.
Cohen’s coefficient corrects for this by comparing observed agreement with the agreement that chance alone would produce, given each coder’s own distribution of codes (Cohen 1960).

Cohen’s kappa — a measure of agreement between two coders on a nominal scale, corrected for chance: \(\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\), where \(p_o\) is the observed share of agreements and \(p_e\) the agreement expected if the two coders assigned categories independently at their own marginal rates. A kappa of 1 is perfect agreement; 0 is agreement no better than chance; negative values are worse than chance.

If coder A puts \(n_{A,k}\) of \(N\) items in category \(k\) and coder B puts \(n_{B,k}\) there, the expected agreement is
\[
p_e = \sum_k \frac{n_{A,k}}{N}\cdot\frac{n_{B,k}}{N}.
\]
Take forty headlines, collapsed into three categories — not geopolitical, threat, act — with coder A’s codes in the rows and coder B’s in the columns, as in Table 7.2:

The coders agree on the diagonal, \(20 + 8 + 5 = 33\) items, so \(p_o = 33/40 = 0.825\). Chance agreement is \((24 \cdot 22 + 10 \cdot 12 + 6 \cdot 6)/40^2 = 684/1600 = 0.4275\). Kappa is therefore \((0.825 - 0.4275)/(1 - 0.4275) \approx 0.69\). An agreement rate of better than four in five shrinks by almost a fifth once chance is removed, because both coders put more than half the headlines in the dominant category, where much of their agreement was to be expected.
What counts as good enough is a convention, and the conventions differ. Landis and Koch proposed a set of labels that have become widely used, under which values between 0.61 and 0.80 are “substantial” (Landis and Koch 1977). Krippendorff, for his alpha — a generalisation that handles more than two coders, missing data and ordinal or interval scales — asks for at least 0.800 before data are relied on, and accepts values from 0.667 only for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff 2018; Hayes and Krippendorff 2007). By the first convention the worked example is respectable; by the second it would support only a tentative claim.

7.6.1 What disagreement is for
The worst thing to do with disagreement is to average it away. Disagreements are where the concept is fuzzy, and they are information. Some will be errors: a coder misread a headline, or forgot a decision rule. Others will reveal that the protocol did not anticipate a case — a headline about sanctions, a cyber operation, a military exercise that might be a build-up or might be routine. Those are the valuable ones. The right response is to revise the protocol, write down the new rule, and then adjudicate.
Any protocol modelled on the GPR categories contains a gap of exactly this kind. Sanctions, export controls and trade wars are not among Caldara and Iacoviello’s eight categories, so a protocol that follows them faithfully must assign such headlines to “not geopolitical” — at best with a flag. Yet a headline about export controls on semiconductors may matter more to a firm’s inputs than one about a distant military exercise. The gap is not a mistake in the GPR index, which measures what it says it measures; it is a reminder that an index built to track war and terrorism may not be the index a firm needs.


7.6.2 Machines as coders
The newest temptation is to hand the coding to a machine: a classifier trained on headlines people have already coded, or a general-purpose language model asked in plain words to apply the protocol. Such systems read latent content better than any dictionary and cost little per headline, but they relocate the problem rather than escape it. A machine coder is a third coder, and its agreement with the humans can be measured with the same coefficient. Automated methods, in Grimmer and Stewart’s words, are no substitute for careful thought and close reading, and require extensive and problem-specific validation (Grimmer and Stewart 2013). A classifier that agrees with people on headlines about elections may disagree on headlines about export controls; only a fresh human-coded sample will say.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.7 Big data: detection, not measurement
text:
7.7 Big data: detection, not measurement
Hand-coded samples are often drawn from automated news monitors, of which the GDELT Project, which turns news media worldwide in many languages into searchable records, is the best known. It is the most visible example of big data in political risk: a source that promises coverage — every country, every day — and speed, without a research assistant reading anything.
The promise is real, and the traps are four. The first is selection. GDELT records what is reported, by the sources it monitors, in the languages it processes. Its coverage of sources has changed over time, so a rising count of articles about a country may mean more sources rather than more events. The second is duplication: one wire-service story republished by hundreds of outlets is counted hundreds of times. The third is machine coding, which misreads irony, quotation and historical reference, and errs in ways that are not random. The fourth is the most seductive: “N = all” is never all, and a very large sample drawn by a biased process is still biased — only more confidently so.
The fourth trap has been formalised. Meng showed that the error of an estimate from a large non-random sample depends on the correlation between being in the sample and the quantity being measured, and that even a tiny such correlation can make a sample of millions worth less than a small random sample (Meng 2018). The parable everyone cites is the story of a search-based model of influenza that, after an initial success, substantially overestimated flu prevalence for long stretches, because the behaviour generating the data changed while the model did not (Lazer et al. 2014). Neither is about geopolitics; both describe what can happen to an event count built from online news.

More data is not better measurement. Millions of machine-coded news records are a sample drawn by a process nobody controls. Forty headlines drawn at random from a well-defined query and coded by two people with a written protocol can be more valid for a specific question — not because forty is more than millions, but because the analyst knows what the forty are.

The working rule for a risk analyst follows. Use big data for detection: something is happening, here, now, and it is worth a closer look. Use small, carefully coded data for measurement: how much is happening, compared with what, and whether it has changed. A monitoring system that flags a spike in news about a firm’s supplier country is doing detection well. A board paper that reports that “risk in the supplier country has doubled” on the strength of the same spike is doing measurement badly.

section: 7.8 Composite indicators and the arithmetic of judgement
text:
7.8 Composite indicators and the arithmetic of judgement
The third measurement task is the one that a multinational is most likely to perform itself: combining several indicators into one number. Country-risk ratings, governance indices, supplier-risk scores and a firm’s own exposure index are all composite indicators. They are attractive for the same reason they are dangerous: they compress several dimensions into one figure that a board can read at a glance, and they hide, in the compression, a series of decisions that determine the ranking.
The standard guide is the handbook produced by the OECD and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre 2008). It sets out ten steps, from the theoretical framework to the presentation of results. Five of them decide most of the outcome.
The theoretical framework says which dimensions of risk the index captures and why. Without one, the index becomes a collection of whatever data were available — which is to say, an index whose content was chosen by the data suppliers rather than by the analyst. For a firm’s exposure index, the natural framework is the five channels: each indicator must be defended as a measure of exposure through a named channel, or it does not belong. An index of a firm’s exposure to sanctions risk, for example, might draw on the share of revenue earned in sanctioned or sanctioning jurisdictions (market access), on the share of critical inputs sourced from them (inputs) and on the banks through which the firm settles in them (finance) — each defensible, and each measuring a different route by which the same political event would reach the accounts.
Missing data is where indices quietly lie. The country GPR indices cover 44 countries; the country EPU indices about twenty. A composite that drops every country missing an indicator will cover only large, well-documented economies — and the countries it silently drops are, very often, the risky ones, about which fewer people write. Imputing a value is a claim about a country nobody measured; flagging the gap is honest and less tidy.
Normalisation puts indicators measured in different units on a common scale. The simplest method, min–max, maps each indicator to the interval from 0 to 1:
\[
x^{*} = \frac{x - \min x}{\max x - \min x}
\qquad\text{or, where higher is safer,}\qquad
x^{*} = \frac{\max x - x}{\max x - \min x}.
\]
The second form matters more than it looks. The Worldwide Governance Indicators’ measure of political stability is scored so that higher means more stable; in a risk index it must be inverted, or a stable country will score as risky. The indicators also changed scale in their 2025 edition, moving to a 0–100 score and recalculating their history, so that values from different editions cannot be mixed; the methodology behind the indicators is set out in Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi (2011). They are themselves composites, pooling many sources in an unobserved-components model that reports a margin of error for every estimate — a discipline most commercial risk scores do not impose on themselves. Other normalisations — z-scores, ranks, distance to a reference country — produce different rankings from the same data, because they treat outliers and gaps differently. Min–max is sensitive to the extremes: a single country with an extraordinary value compresses everyone else into a narrow band.
Weighting and aggregation combine the normalised indicators. The usual form is a weighted average,
\[
CI = \frac{\sum_j w_j \, x^{*}_j}{\sum_j w_j},
\]
and the weights can be equal, derived statistically (from principal components, say), or set by experts. Each choice is defensible and none is neutral. Equal weights are a judgement that every dimension matters equally, which is rarely what anyone believes. Statistical weights reward the indicators that move together, which may simply be the redundant ones. Expert weights encode the expert.
The aggregation rule carries a further assumption that is easy to miss.

Compensability — the property of an aggregation rule under which a high score on one dimension can offset a low score on another. Additive aggregation is fully compensatory: a country with excellent governance and an active war can average to “medium”. Geometric aggregation is partially compensatory, penalising unbalanced profiles; non-compensatory rules rank countries without allowing any trade-off at all.

For a risk index, full compensability is often the wrong assumption. A firm does not experience the average of a country’s risks; it experiences the worst of them that touches its operations. Excellent contract enforcement does not compensate for a plant inside a war zone. Additive aggregation remains the default because it is transparent, but whoever uses it should show the profile behind each score.

From the archive · The Human Development Index, 1990 and 2010
The most influential composite indicator of the past half-century was designed to argue with a single number. The first Human Development Report, published by the United Nations Development Programme in 1990 under the direction of Mahbub ul Haq, proposed the Human Development Index as an alternative to ranking countries by income per head (United Nations Development Programme 1990). It combined three dimensions — a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living — each normalised against minimum and maximum values, and averaged them with equal weights. It was a simplification built to change a conversation, and it did.
Twenty years later the 2010 report changed the aggregation from an arithmetic to a geometric mean of the three dimension indices and revised the indicators of education and income (United Nations Development Programme 2010). The reason given was compensability: under the arithmetic mean, a country could make up for poor health with high income, one for one; under the geometric mean, poor performance in one dimension weighs more heavily. The change re-ranked countries. Ravallion then showed that the new formula implied trade-offs between longevity and income that few would accept if they were stated openly — in effect, valuations of an extra year of life that varied enormously with a country’s income, and were very low in the poorest countries (Ravallion 2012).
The weights and the aggregation rule were value judgements; changing them changed the ranking; and the implicit prices they carried became visible only when someone did the algebra. A firm’s exposure index embeds trade-offs of the same kind, and the board deserves to see them stated.

section: 7.9 Sensitivity: the ranking that one weight overturns
text:
7.9 Sensitivity: the ranking that one weight overturns
The last of the decisive steps is the one most often skipped. Sensitivity analysis asks how much the results move when the choices change: a different normalisation, different weights, a different treatment of missing data, a different aggregation rule. Saisana, Saltelli and Tarantola set out how to do this systematically, by treating each methodological choice as an uncertain input and examining the distribution of ranks it produces (Saisana, Saltelli, and Tarantola 2005). The simplest version needs no special software. Record the ranking under equal weights; then under each indicator alone; then count how many countries move by more than a few places. A country that stays near the top under every reasonable choice is robustly high-risk. A country whose rank swings from fifth to twenty-fifth depending on one weight is not “fifth”; it is a country about which the index has no firm opinion.
This is why a composite worth showing to a board should be presented with weights the reader can move, or at least with the rankings that alternative weights would produce. The point is not interactivity for its own sake. It is that a composite which hides its weights is an opinion dressed as a measurement, and a composite whose weights are visible and adjustable is an argument the reader can test. A board that sees a supplier country fall from first to ninth when one weight is halved has learnt that the decision rests on a judgement about that indicator, not on the index.

7.9.1 Two indicators, forty-four countries
A small composite shows how quickly these choices bite. Take the 44 countries for which Caldara and Iacoviello publish a country index, and combine two indicators: the average country GPR for 2025, which measures the share of newspaper articles that discuss geopolitical tension and mention the country, and the political stability score of the Worldwide Governance Indicators for 2024, from the 2025 edition, inverted so that a higher value means less stability. Normalise each by min–max, and average them with a weight \(w\) on GPR and \(1-w\) on instability. Nothing could be simpler, and almost nothing about the result is stable (Figure 7.5 and Table 7.3).
The two indicators barely agree to begin with: across the 44 countries, the correlation between the GPR ranking and the instability ranking is 0.09. Under GPR alone the United States is the riskiest country in the set; under instability alone it is twentieth. Venezuela is first on instability and nineteenth on GPR; Tunisia sixth on instability and last on GPR. With equal weights, the United States comes first, Israel second and Russia third. Move the weight on GPR from a quarter to three quarters and 13 of the 44 countries move by more than five places; the United Kingdom moves from twentieth to fourth, China from nineteenth to sixth, Germany from twenty-third to twelfth.

The cause of the movements is the lesson. The country GPR measures how often the newspapers write about a country in a geopolitical context, and the newspapers write about the United States, the United Kingdom, China, France and Germany as actors — the states that send forces, impose sanctions and convene summits — as well as about the places where conflict happens. A validity problem at the indicator link has become a ranking problem at the aggregation link. Min–max normalisation then amplifies it. In 2025 the United States’ country index averaged 3.61 and the median of the 44 was 0.16, so that 38 of the 44 countries sit in the bottom quarter of the GPR range once it is scaled from 0 to 1. The GPR component separates a few heavily reported countries from everyone else and says almost nothing about the differences among the rest; a z-score or a rank would produce another ranking again.
The top is robust: Israel and Russia are in the first three under every weight from a quarter to three quarters. The middle is not. Whether China ranks above Colombia, or the United Kingdom above India, is decided by a weight nobody could defend to the first decimal. A board shown only the equal-weight column has been shown an opinion about the weight.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.10 A short review of the literature
text:
7.10 A short review of the literature

Content analysis as a social-science method was codified in the mid-twentieth century. Berelson (1952) gave the classic definition centred on manifest content, and George (1959) reconstructed the wartime analysis of enemy propaganda that showed both the power and the dangers of inference from text. Krippendorff (2018) is the standard modern treatment, recasting the method around replicable and valid inference and setting out the reliability apparatus; Hayes and Krippendorff (2007) make the case for Krippendorff’s alpha as a general standard. The chance-corrected agreement coefficient is Cohen (1960), and the labels most often attached to its values are Landis and Koch (1977).
Grimmer and Stewart (2013) is the essential guide to automated analysis of political texts, and its insistence on problem-specific validation is the spine of this chapter. Gentzkow, Kelly, and Taddy (2019) survey text as data in economics. In finance, Tetlock (2007) showed that dictionary measures of media tone carry information about markets, and Loughran and McDonald (2011) showed how badly general-purpose dictionaries misread specialised documents.
The three indices at the centre of the chapter are Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) for geopolitical risk, Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016) for economic policy uncertainty and Hassan et al. (2019) for firm-level political risk. On big data, Lazer et al. (2014) is the cautionary tale and Meng (2018) the formal account of why sample size does not rescue a biased selection process.
Composite indicators have their own methodological literature. OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre (2008) is the practitioner’s handbook and Saisana, Saltelli, and Tarantola (2005) the statement of sensitivity and uncertainty analysis as a quality test. Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi (2011) document the Worldwide Governance Indicators, a composite of composites. The Human Development Index (United Nations Development Programme 1990, 2010) and the critique of its implicit trade-offs in Ravallion (2012) are the clearest case study of how aggregation rules carry value judgements.

title: 7  Measuring Risk: How a Political Judgement Becomes a Number
section: 7.11 What the numbers do not license
text:
7.11 What the numbers do not license
Each measure in this chapter comes with a sentence it does not license. Where two of them part company, the question is not which is right but which link of which chain explains the gap.
The line of average firm-level political risk does not tell a particular multinational how much political risk it faces. It is an average over American listed firms, and the central finding of the paper that built it is that most political risk is specific to the firm — precisely the variation an average removes. A board can use the line to see when political uncertainty was high for corporate America as a whole; it cannot use it to see its own exposure, which would require scoring its own calls, or at least those of its closest peers.
A hand-coded index of the news about a country, however carefully its coders agree, does not license a claim about how geopolitical that country’s situation is. A few dozen headlines from a news monitor that leans towards English-language media, coded against a protocol that places sanctions outside geopolitics, measure what one slice of the press said, filtered through one theory of what counts. What a good kappa licenses is a statement about how reliably two trained readers can apply that protocol — and the list of disagreements licenses something more valuable, which is a map of the places where the protocol must change before anyone relies on it.
A composite exposure index does not license a ranking presented as fact. It licenses a ranking under stated weights, together with the weight that would overturn it. That is less than a board usually wants, and more than it usually gets.
The argument of this chapter can be compressed into a five-part audit, to be put to every risk score a multinational builds or buys: what concept, from which sources, coded by whom or by what, normalised and weighted how, and how sensitive to each of those choices. None requires a statistician; each requires only that the score’s makers have written down what they did. The scores that survive the audit are not thereby true. They are measurements — numbers whose errors can be named and whose disagreements with other numbers can be traced to a decision someone took. A score that cannot answer the five questions is somebody’s opinion, with decimals; and the danger of such a score is not that the opinion is wrong, but that the decimals make it impossible to argue with.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
text:
8.1 The war that was supposed to happen
For most of the past three decades, the public conversation about cyberspace and international politics has been conducted in the future tense. A “cyber Pearl Harbor” would switch off a country’s power grid; a handful of skilled operators would humble a great power; the next war would be won or lost before a shot was fired. The scenarios were vivid, and they were not absurd: modern economies do run on networked systems, and those systems can be broken. What the scenarios lacked was a record. They were claims about what could happen, offered in the absence of systematic evidence about what had.
The opposite caricature is just as easy to state. On this view cyber operations are simply crime and espionage conducted with better tools — a nuisance for security departments, of no strategic consequence, and no business of a book on geopolitics. It, too, is a claim about evidence, and it, too, is usually made without any.
This chapter takes the question to the data. It does so through the work of Brandon Valeriano and Ryan Maness, who built a dataset of cyber incidents between rival states and asked what the record actually shows (Valeriano and Maness 2015), and through the argument of Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman that the networks globalisation built are not flat, and that states with jurisdiction over their hubs can turn them into instruments of coercion (Farrell and Newman 2019). The two works answer different questions. The first asks how states use offensive cyber operations against each other. The second asks how states use the architecture of the global economy — including its digital architecture — to watch and to deny. A multinational needs both answers, because it sits inside the architecture and in the path of the operations.
The question for the firm is narrower and more practical than the question for the strategist. It is not whether cyberspace is a new domain of war. It is through which channels inter-state rivalry in cyberspace reaches a firm’s operations, and how its decision architecture should absorb it. The answer, this chapter argues, is that the firm is rarely the intended target of strategic cyber operations, frequently their collateral, and increasingly a piece of the infrastructure over which states compete.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.2 Three activities that look alike
text:
8.2 Three activities that look alike
Three kinds of activity are routinely run together under the heading “cyber attack”, and the first task is to separate them.
Espionage steals information: state secrets, negotiating positions, intellectual property, the personal data of officials. Its typical actors are intelligence services and their contractors, and its typical intrusion — into a ministry, a defence supplier or a law firm advising on a merger — is designed never to be noticed. Disruption and degradation interrupt or damage systems: a denial-of-service attack that floods a ministry’s website, malware that wipes the disks of a company’s computers, an operation that manipulates an industrial control system. Its actors are military and intelligence units and the proxies they sponsor. Crime extracts money: ransomware that encrypts a hospital’s records, fraud against a bank’s payment systems. Its actors are criminal groups.

Cyber operation — the use of computer code or network access by an organised actor to obtain information from, disrupt, degrade or manipulate a target’s information systems. Espionage, disruption and crime are all cyber operations; they differ in purpose and actor, not in technique. The same intrusion may serve any of the three.

The boundaries blur, and the blurring is itself a geopolitical fact. States tolerate criminal groups that operate from their territory against foreign targets, hire them, shelter them, and occasionally use their tools. An intrusion that begins as espionage leaves access that can later be used for disruption. A ransomware campaign run by a criminal group may serve a state’s purposes by sowing disorder in a rival’s economy, without the state having ordered it. When a ransomware attack by a criminal group believed to operate from Russia forced the shutdown of the Colonial Pipeline in the United States in May 2021 (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency 2023), it was crime in its motive and geopolitics in its consequences: the question of what the Russian state knew, tolerated or could have prevented became a matter between governments.
For a multinational the distinction matters because the three activities call for different responses. Espionage is a threat to the firm’s intellectual property and its negotiating position, and the defence is largely technical and organisational. Disruption is a threat to its operations, and the defence includes resilience — the ability to keep working when systems fail. Crime is a threat to its cash and its reputation, and it is the one where law enforcement, insurers and the firm’s own willingness to pay become part of the calculation. A risk register that lists “cyber” as a single line has not yet done the first piece of analysis.

From the archive · Estonia, 2007
In April 2007 the Estonian government moved a Soviet-era war memorial, the Bronze Soldier, from the centre of Tallinn to a military cemetery. The decision provoked protests by members of the country’s Russian-speaking minority and an angry response from Moscow. Over the following weeks a wave of distributed denial-of-service attacks hit Estonian government websites, banks, newspapers and political parties. Estonia, among the most digitised societies in Europe, found its online services intermittently unreachable.
Estonian officials pointed to Russia. The Russian government denied involvement, and the public record never established a chain of command; much of the traffic came from botnets and from individuals mobilised on Russian-language forums. The episode thus contained, in compressed form, nearly every feature that later analysts would identify in state cyber conflict: an existing political rivalry, an operation of low technical sophistication and limited physical harm, high political salience, and attribution that remained contested.
Its institutional legacy was substantial. NATO’s Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence was established in Tallinn the following year, and under its auspices a group of international lawyers produced the Tallinn Manual, an attempt to state how existing international law applies to cyber operations (Schmitt 2013). The episode was widely described at the time as the first cyber war. With hindsight it looks more like the first clear case of what Valeriano and Maness would call restraint: a rival state’s displeasure expressed through disruption that stopped well short of destruction.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.3 The restraint thesis
text:
8.3 The restraint thesis
Valeriano and Maness built their dataset around a simple design choice that shapes everything they found. They did not try to catalogue every cyber operation in the world. They took pairs of states with a history of enduring hostility — rivals, in the sense the international-conflict literature has used for decades — and recorded the cyber incidents between them. The unit is the incident, nested in campaigns; the population is rival dyads; the evidence is public. The dataset has since been extended as the Dyadic Cyber Incident and Campaign Data (DCID), whose version 2.0 covers incidents beginning between 2000 and 2020 (Maness et al. 2022).

Cyber incident (in DCID) — an individual cyber operation launched by one state against another within a rival dyad, with a start date, a method, a target type, an objective and a severity score. Incidents can be grouped into campaigns, sustained series of operations with a common purpose. The unit is the incident between rivals, not the operation in general.

The choice of rivals as the population is a theoretical commitment, not a convenience. The study of international conflict has long found that a small number of pairs of states account for a large share of militarised disputes, and that these enduring rivalries have their own dynamics: hostility persists, crises recur, and each side interprets the other’s moves in the light of a long history. If cyber operations are a new instrument of old conflicts, rivalries are where they should appear; if they are something genuinely new — an instrument that lets any state hurt any other cheaply — they should appear outside rivalries too. Restricting the data to rivals makes the first hypothesis testable and the second invisible — a limitation to which this chapter returns when the rival-dyad record is set beside a wider one.
From that record they drew four propositions.
The first is restraint. States use cyber operations far less often, and far less destructively, than the “cyber war” narrative predicts. Most incidents in the data are of low severity: defacements of websites, denial-of-service attacks, espionage. Operations that destroy physical property or take lives are rare. The image of cyberspace as a domain of constant, escalating attack does not survive contact with a systematic count.
The public release of the data lets the claim be checked directly (Figure 8.1). Of the 433 incidents in the September 2022 release of DCID, 393 — nine in ten — are coded 2, 3 or 4 on the severity scale: harassment and disruption, the theft of information from one network, or widespread intrusion into several. Eighteen are coded 5, for intrusions that attempted damage, and five are coded 6, the level the codebook reserves for widespread destruction in a network critical to national security. Those five are the canonical cases: the two Stuxnet entries against Iran, starting in 2009 and attributed one to the United States and one to Israel; the Shamoon wiper and the attack on the gas producer RasGas, both attributed to Iran and directed at Saudi Arabia in 2012; and the reported American effort to sabotage North Korean missile launches, coded for 2015. Nothing in two decades is coded 7 or above — the levels at which the codebook places deaths, the disruption of a national economy and the destruction of critical infrastructure.






Figure 8.1: Nine in ten publicly attributed cyber incidents between rival states sit at 2–4 on a ten-point severity scale, and none above 6. Incidents beginning 2000–2020 by severity, with the codebook’s labels. Source: Dyadic Cyber Incident and Campaign Data, version 2.0 (September 2022 release), and its Codebook 2.0.



The scale is worth reading for what it ranks low. The operation that cost firms more than any other in the record, NotPetya, appears twice: once against Ukraine, coded 5, and once against the United States, coded 4 — below Stuxnet and Shamoon. The WannaCry ransomware of 2017, attributed to North Korea, is coded 4 in both its American and its British entries, although it shut down hospital services in Britain. The scale measures harm as a state experiences it, against networks critical to national security, and that is the right scale for testing a theory of how states fight. It is not a scale of cost to the firms that are in the way, and an analyst who sorted incidents by it to rank commercial exposure would have the order wrong.

Cyber restraint — the empirical pattern, and the theoretical argument, that states with offensive cyber capabilities use them sparingly and at low severity against their rivals, holding back the most destructive options. Restraint is a claim about strategic severity, not about frequency of nuisance or about commercial cost.

The second is that cyber conflict follows regional rivalries. The dyads that account for most of the incidents are those that were already hostile before anyone had a network: the United States and China, Russia and its neighbours and the West, Israel and Iran, India and Pakistan, the two Koreas. Cyber operations do not create new conflicts; they are a tool in old ones. That finding matters for anyone who expected the low cost of entry to cyber operations to flatten the international hierarchy. The states that are most active in cyberspace are, by and large, the states that were already contending.
The concentration is easy to state in numbers (Figure 8.2). The 433 incidents fall into 52 directed pairs of initiator and target, and the five largest — China against the United States (59 incidents), Russia against the United States (40), North Korea against South Korea (37), Russia against Ukraine (28) and Iran against the United States (21) — account for 43 per cent of the total; the ten largest for 61 per cent. Four initiators, China (115 incidents), Russia (113), Iran (63) and North Korea (59), account for 81 per cent of the record, and the United States is the target of 32 per cent of it. The United States appears as initiator in 24 incidents, and Israel in ten. Those numbers carry the warning set out below about attribution: they are the operations that someone chose to make public and that the coders could attribute, and the states with the most capable intelligence services and the most active public attribution are, unsurprisingly, more often found as victims than as perpetrators.






Figure 8.2: The record of cyber conflict between rivals is dominated by a few old rivalries: the five largest directed pairs account for 43 per cent of all incidents. The twelve largest pairs, 2000–2020, by initiator. Source: Dyadic Cyber Incident and Campaign Data, version 2.0.



The third proposition explains the first: why states hold back. The fourth is that cyber operations have limited coercive effect. They rarely change the target’s behaviour. They are better at signalling displeasure and at gathering intelligence than at compelling a rival to do something it would otherwise not do — a conclusion that the same authors developed at greater length in later work on cyber strategy (Valeriano, Jensen, and Maness 2018).
The restraint thesis did not arrive in an empty field. Thomas Rid had argued, provocatively, that cyber war in the sense of an act of force that is violent, instrumental and political had never occurred, and that what was called cyber war was better understood as sabotage, espionage and subversion — old activities in a new medium (Rid 2012, 2013). Erik Gartzke made a related argument from the logic of force: an attack that cannot be followed up by conventional power changes nothing durable, so cyber operations are likely to be adjuncts to force rather than substitutes for it (Gartzke 2013). Lucas Kello took the opposite position, arguing that the cyber revolution genuinely strained the concepts of international relations because it blurred war and peace into a condition of permanent, sub-threshold “unpeace” (Kello 2013, 2017). Valeriano and Maness’s contribution was to bring data to an argument that had been conducted largely through concepts and anecdotes, and the data came down closer to Rid and Gartzke than to the prophets of catastrophe.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.4 Why states hold back
text:
8.4 Why states hold back
The reasons for restraint are worth taking one at a time, because each has an analogue in the firm’s own calculation.
Escalation. A destructive cyber operation against a rival invites a response, and the response need not stay in cyberspace. A state that switches off a rival’s grid has made a move whose consequences it cannot control. In a relationship where both sides have conventional and sometimes nuclear forces, the incentive to stay below the threshold that would provoke them is strong.
Revelation. A cyber capability depends on a vulnerability the target has not fixed. Using it reveals it, and once revealed it can be patched — in the target’s systems and everyone else’s. The most sophisticated capabilities are therefore wasting assets, worth more held in reserve than spent.
Blowback. Malicious code, once released, can be captured, analysed and reused. A weapon that can be reverse-engineered and turned back on its maker, or on the maker’s allies and firms, is a weapon to be used with care.
Access. The value of being inside a rival’s networks is often greater than the value of damaging them. A state that can read a rival’s communications has every reason not to do anything that would alert the rival to its presence. Espionage, in this sense, restrains disruption.
These incentives are not the whole story. Ben Buchanan has argued that intrusions made for defensive purposes — to understand a rival’s capabilities, or to pre-position against a future threat — look identical, from the target’s side, to preparation for attack, and that this creates a security dilemma in which each side’s prudence alarms the other (Buchanan 2017). Restraint in the use of destructive operations is compatible with constant, mutual intrusion, and the intrusions themselves are a source of instability.
The war in Ukraine has tested the restraint thesis harder than anything in the dataset, which ends in 2020. Russian cyber operations against Ukraine have been extensive since 2014, and they intensified around the full-scale invasion of February 2022. The best systematic study of the earlier period found that cyber operations had little discernible effect on events on the battlefield (Kostyuk and Zhukov 2019), which is consistent with the fourth proposition: cyber operations are weak instruments of compulsion even in war. Whether the restraint thesis holds as of today is an open question. A pattern measured to 2020 is evidence about 2000–2020, and the war has supplied episodes that sit awkwardly within it.
One of them began in the first hours of the invasion. On 24 February 2022 an operation against the KA-SAT satellite network operated by the American company Viasat disabled large numbers of the modems its customers used in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe. The apparent target was Ukrainian military and government communications. Among the collateral casualties was the remote monitoring and control of wind farms in central Europe, whose operators used the same service. In May 2022 the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States attributed the operation to Russia (UK Government 2022). The episode is consistent with restraint in the narrow sense — it was an adjunct to a conventional invasion, not a substitute for one — and it is a warning about everything the restraint thesis does not cover. A commercial satellite network was a target because the Ukrainian state relied on it, and the firms that suffered had no connection to the war except that they were customers of the same hub.
The most famous exception proves the rule in an instructive way. The operation later known as Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, sabotaged centrifuges at Iran’s uranium-enrichment plant at Natanz by manipulating the industrial control systems that ran them. It was widely attributed to the United States and Israel, neither of which has formally acknowledged it. It is the clearest case in the public record of code causing physical destruction to a rival’s strategic asset, and it fits the restraint thesis better than the catastrophe narrative: it was narrowly targeted, designed to look like malfunction rather than attack, and aimed at delaying a programme rather than at provoking a war. It also illustrates blowback. The code escaped the plant’s isolated network, spread to computers around the world, and was analysed in detail by security researchers, so that its techniques became available to everyone. For firms, the lesson was that industrial control systems — the machinery of plants, pipelines and utilities — were now a target class, and that the code designed to attack one of them could end up on their own networks.

Low strategic severity is not low commercial cost. An operation that barely registers on a scale of harm between states — a wiper that destroys no infrastructure and kills no one — can halt a company’s production for weeks. The restraint thesis is about what states do to each other. The firm’s question is what happens to the firms that happen to be in the way.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.5 Weaponised interdependence
text:
8.5 Weaponised interdependence
Valeriano and Maness study offensive operations. Farrell and Newman study something quieter and, for a multinational, probably more consequential: the way in which the networks of the global economy can be used by the states that sit at their centre (Farrell and Newman 2019).
Their starting observation is that the networks globalisation built — for finance, for communications, for the internet’s physical and logical infrastructure — are not flat meshes in which every node is equal. They are highly asymmetric, with a few hubs through which most traffic passes. Network economics explains why: hubs are efficient, and efficiency attracts more traffic, which makes the hub more central still. The internationalisation of the 1990s was conducted on the assumption that this centralisation was a technical fact with no political content. Farrell and Newman’s argument is that the assumption was wrong. A state that has jurisdiction over a hub can use it.

Panopticon effect — the use of jurisdiction over a network hub to see what flows through it: to gather information about the activities of other states, firms and individuals whose traffic passes through the hub.


Chokepoint effect — the use of jurisdiction over a network hub to deny others access to it: to cut a bank out of a payment system, a firm out of a software supply, a country out of a market for critical components.

The two effects need each other. The panopticon tells a state where to apply the chokepoint, and the chokepoint gives the panopticon its teeth. Farrell and Newman’s cases make both concrete. The disclosures by Edward Snowden in 2013 showed the extent to which American intelligence agencies had used the concentration of global internet traffic and data storage in American firms and on American territory to collect information at scale — the panopticon. The disconnection of sanctioned Iranian banks from the SWIFT financial-messaging network in 2012, after the European Union adopted the necessary legal measures, showed how a hub located in one jurisdiction could be used to deny a whole country’s banking system its normal connection to the world — the chokepoint.
The implication for a multinational is uncomfortable in two ways. The first is that the firm’s exposure to geopolitical risk depends on where the hubs it uses are located and whose law applies to them. A firm whose payments clear through one jurisdiction, whose data are stored with providers subject to another, and whose software updates arrive from a third has three sets of exposure to the coercive choices of three states, most of which have nothing to do with the firm.
The second is more uncomfortable still: the firm itself can be the hub. A cloud provider, a payment network, a telecommunications operator, a maker of widely used software — each is infrastructure that its home state can watch through or weaponise, and that rival states therefore have reason to treat as a target, to exclude, or to replace with a domestic alternative. A firm in that position is not a bystander to geopolitical competition. It is part of the terrain. This is the bridge to sanctions in Chapter 10, where the chokepoint becomes a legal instrument, and to space in Chapter 11, where the hubs are in orbit.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.6 Attribution: evidence about evidence
text:
8.6 Attribution: evidence about evidence
Every dataset of state cyber operations rests on an act of attribution. Somebody has to say who did it. And attribution in cyberspace has four properties that make it unlike the identification of the attacker in almost any other kind of conflict event.

Attribution — the identification of the actor responsible for a cyber operation, at three levels: the machines used, the individuals or groups who operated them, and the state, if any, that directed or sponsored them. Public attribution is the decision to announce the third.

It is slow. Forensic analysis takes weeks or months; public attribution by governments often comes a year or more after the event. It is probabilistic. Technical indicators — the code, the infrastructure, the working hours of the operators, the language settings left in a file — can be faked, borrowed or reused, and a careful operator plants false ones. It is political. Governments decide when to attribute publicly, to whom, and with how much of their evidence, and they decide in the light of their relations with the accused state and their wish to protect their own sources. And it is selective. What is attributed publicly is what someone wanted known.
Rid and Buchanan put the point sharply: attribution is what states make of it (Rid and Buchanan 2015). It is not a technical fact waiting to be discovered but a judgement, assembled from technical, operational and strategic evidence, and communicated for a purpose. Lindsay offered a partial corrective: for the most consequential operations the set of capable actors is small, and the attribution problem is therefore less severe than it is for routine intrusions — which is one reason deterrence of major attacks remains possible (Lindsay 2015). Both views lead to the same conclusion about data.
An event dataset of cyber operations is a record of public attributions, not a record of operations. That sentence is the most important caveat attached to every count in this chapter. It has predictable consequences for what the data show. States that attribute publicly — mostly Western democracies, with active security services and a free press — appear more often as victims than states that do not. Operations by allies against each other are rarely attributed in public and are therefore nearly invisible. Operations that succeeded in remaining undetected are, by definition, absent. A dyad with no incidents in the data may be a dyad with no operations, or a dyad in which neither side chose to say anything.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.7 When the firm is collateral
text:
8.7 When the firm is collateral
The restraint thesis concerns the intentions of states. The cost to firms is driven by something else: the technical reach of what states release.

From the archive · NotPetya, June 2017
On 27 June 2017, the eve of a Ukrainian public holiday, malware spread through the update mechanism of a Ukrainian accounting program widely used by businesses operating in the country. It looked like ransomware, displaying a demand for payment, but its encryption could not be reversed: it was a wiper dressed as a ransom note. Within hours it had spread beyond Ukraine through the internal networks of any company that ran the software at a Ukrainian site. In February 2018 the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom, among others, publicly attributed the operation to the Russian military.
The apparent target was Ukraine. The victims included some of the largest firms in the world. The shipping company Maersk lost the use of systems across its global operations. The pharmaceutical company Merck and the food company Mondelez reported very large losses, as did logistics and manufacturing firms in many countries. None of them had a quarrel with anyone; they had a subsidiary, an office or a supplier in Ukraine, running a program everybody used (Greenberg 2019).
The aftermath carried a second lesson. When the companies claimed under their property insurance, insurers invoked the war exclusions that such policies had carried for generations, arguing that an operation by a state’s military was an act of war. The litigation lasted years and did not go uniformly the insurers’ way; in Merck’s case, New Jersey courts held that the traditional exclusion, written with armed conflict in mind, did not cover the attack. The market’s response was to write explicit exclusions for state-backed cyber operations into its contracts, which the Lloyd’s market required from 2023. The effect is that a firm’s cyber cover may now end exactly where geopolitics begins.

Three lessons follow for the firm. The first is that proximity in cyberspace is technical, not political. Firms were hit by NotPetya because they ran a piece of software in a country at war, not because anyone chose them. A firm’s exposure to a state’s cyber operations depends on its network architecture — what it connects to, what it updates from, what its subsidiaries can reach — as much as on its political profile.
The second is that insurance is not a backstop. A risk transfer that excludes the scenario the board is most worried about does not transfer that risk. The question to ask of a cyber policy is not whether it covers “cyber attacks” but what it says about operations attributed to states — and who decides the attribution.
The third is that the board owns it. Securities regulators increasingly require listed firms to disclose material cyber incidents and to describe how their boards oversee cyber risk. In the United States, rules adopted in 2023 require listed companies to report material incidents promptly and to describe their risk management and governance of cybersecurity in their annual reports (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission 2023). The geopolitical part of cyber risk — the part that arises from the rivalry of states — is thereby made a matter of corporate governance, whatever the firm’s own view of it.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.8 Digital sovereignty and the splintering network
text:
8.8 Digital sovereignty and the splintering network
Weaponised interdependence has a defensive mirror. States that fear the panopticon and the chokepoint of others respond by asserting control over the networks within their own jurisdiction: where data must be stored, who may access them, which foreign equipment may be installed, which vendors may operate. The vocabulary varies — digital sovereignty, data localisation, trusted vendors, technological self-reliance — and the effect is the same. The single global network on which the internationalisation of the 1990s assumed firms could operate is splintering into jurisdictions with different rules.
Three instruments matter most for a multinational. Data-localisation and transfer rules require that certain data be stored within a country or restrict their movement abroad; the invalidation by the Court of Justice of the European Union in 2020 of the framework that governed transfers of personal data from the European Union to the United States showed how quickly a legal basis for a firm’s data architecture can disappear. Security reviews and vendor bans exclude foreign suppliers from critical networks; the restrictions imposed on Huawei’s telecommunications equipment by the United States and a number of its allies from 2019 onward forced operators to redesign and in some cases to strip out networks they had already built. Access laws give governments the power to compel firms under their jurisdiction to hand over data, including data stored abroad; the United States’ CLOUD Act of 2018 is the best-known example, and it sits awkwardly beside European data-protection law.
For the firm, these instruments generate three kinds of cost. Duplication: separate data centres or cloud regions per jurisdiction, separate supply chains for network equipment, separate compliance regimes. Conflicting obligations: one state’s law requires a disclosure that another’s forbids, and the firm must choose which to break. Vendor risk: a supplier banned in one market may be mandatory, or at least dominant, in another, so that a single global architecture becomes impossible. None of these costs arises from a cyber operation. All of them arise from the geopolitics of cyberspace.

title: 8  Cyber Geopolitics: Restraint, Rivals and Weaponised Networks
section: 8.9 Where cyber risk sits in the firm
text:
8.9 Where cyber risk sits in the firm
The five channels through which geopolitical risk reaches a multinational help locate cyber risk precisely. It runs most obviously through data and operations: the operation that halts production, the localisation rule that forces a redesign. It runs through assets and people, when intellectual property is stolen or staff in a jurisdiction are compelled to provide access. It runs through finance, when insurers exclude state-backed operations and when payment hubs become chokepoints. It runs through inputs, when a vendor is banned or a software supply chain is compromised — NotPetya travelled through a software update. And it runs through market access, when a firm is excluded from a market as a security risk, or when its home state’s use of the firm as a hub makes it unwelcome abroad.
Inside the firm, the risk is distributed across several actors, and the distribution is part of the problem. The board sets risk appetite and oversees disclosure; its distinctive question is which state actors would want our data or our downtime, and why? The chief information security officer turns threat intelligence into controls and owns incident response, but typically reports through a technology function with limited geopolitical analysis. The chief risk officer is the natural integrator of cyber risk with country, sanctions and supply-chain risk — the view this book takes. The insurer prices the risk and, increasingly, draws the line at state-backed operations. And regulators impose disclosure, localisation and vendor rules from outside. A firm in which each of these actors holds a piece of the picture and nobody holds the whole has a decision architecture designed for crime and espionage, not for geopolitics.
What should change for a firm with a plant in a country that sits in one of the densest cells of the rivalry matrix? Not, in the first instance, its technology. The first change is to the map: an inventory of which systems at that site connect to which systems elsewhere, which software is updated from which vendors, and which data cross which borders — because it is along those connections that an operation aimed at a government travels into a firm. The second is to segmentation: a subsidiary in a contested jurisdiction whose network can reach the group’s core systems is a bridge for anyone who compromises it, and the cheapest geopolitical control a firm can buy is often a wall between the two. The third is to contracts: what the insurance policy says about operations attributed to states, what the cloud provider’s terms say about government access in each jurisdiction, and what suppliers have agreed about notifying the firm when they are compromised. The fourth is to governance: who in the firm asks, before an investment rather than after an incident, which states would want the firm’s data or its downtime.

section: 8.10 What the record shows, and how it was made
text:
8.10 What the record shows, and how it was made
The descriptive picture at the heart of Valeriano and Maness’s book — incidents by year, by method and by severity, and the matrix of who targets whom — can be rebuilt from the public release of DCID, and the codebook repays reading because it is where the concepts of this chapter become columns.
The unit is one incident between an initiating state and a target state within a rival dyad. The dyad’s two states are recorded in the order of their Correlates of War codes, so that the first state of the pair is not necessarily the initiator; the initiator is recorded separately, and the target is whichever state of the dyad did not initiate. The method is coded on a scale that runs from vandalism through denial of service and network intrusion to network infiltration, with sub-codes for kinds of malicious software. Severity is coded on a scale the codebook defines from 0 to 10, of which the released file uses only the values 0 to 6 — a discrepancy that, if the codebook’s scale applies, is itself consistent with restraint: in two decades of rivalry, nothing in the record reaches the upper part of the scale. The type of target distinguishes private and non-state targets from governmental ones, civilian and military, and the objective distinguishes disruption, short- and long-term espionage and degradation. The September 2022 release contains 433 incidents with start dates from September 2000 to January 2021.
Two properties of the data follow directly from the arguments above. The first is that the population is rival dyads. A cell of the initiator × target matrix that is empty does not mean “no cyber conflict”; it means “no rivalry in the data”, because pairs of states that are not coded as rivals never enter. The second is that the incidents are public attributions. The matrix is therefore a picture of who has been publicly accused of operating against whom — itself a geopolitical artefact, shaped by which governments attribute and when.
The record does say something about what the operations were for and whom they hit, and both answers matter to a firm (Table 8.1). Espionage, short- or long-term, is the objective of 263 incidents, three in five; disruption of 120; and degradation — the deliberate damage of a target’s systems — of 50. And 175 of the 433 incidents, 40 per cent, are coded as directed at private or non-state targets rather than at governments or militaries. Even in a dataset built to study conflict between states, the target was a company or another non-state body in two incidents in five.

In the first decade of the record, vandalism and denial-of-service attacks — the defacements and floods of the Estonian kind — made up a third of the incidents.
