title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.9 The firm in the middle
text:
10.9 The firm in the middle
Sanctions are aimed at states, governments and the people who run them. They are implemented by firms. Banks, exporters, shippers and insurers decide, transaction by transaction, whether a payment, shipment or contract falls within the rules, and bear severe penalties if they decide wrongly. The firm is therefore not a bystander to sanctions policy. It is its executor, and its executor of last resort.

10.9.1 Lists, ownership and the perimeter
Each sending jurisdiction maintains its own legal architecture. In the United States, sanctions programmes rest mostly on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 and are administered by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, whose Specially Designated Nationals list is the most consulted list in global commerce. In the European Union, restrictive measures are adopted by Council decision and given effect by regulations binding every person and firm in the Union. In Canada, they rest on the Special Economic Measures Act, the United Nations Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act. The lists overlap but do not coincide, and a firm operating across jurisdictions must satisfy all of them.
The list is only the beginning of the perimeter. Under the US “50 percent rule”, an entity owned, directly or indirectly, 50 percent or more in aggregate by listed persons is itself treated as blocked, whether or not it appears on any list; EU guidance extends the restrictions to entities owned or controlled by listed persons, with control judged on a range of indicators. A firm must therefore screen not only its counterparties but their owners, and their owners’ owners, through chains of holding companies that may be designed to obscure them.

Compliance perimeter — the set of counterparties, transactions, goods and jurisdictions a firm must treat as restricted in order to comply with every sanctions regime that applies to it. It is wider than any list: it includes entities owned or controlled by listed persons, goods restricted by end use, and the jurisdictions whose rules reach the firm through its nationality, its currency, its banks or its inputs.



10.9.2 Diversion and the duty to look downstream
Sanctions on goods have always leaked through third countries. After 2022 the leak ran through distributors in countries that did not apply the measures, which re-exported to Russia goods that had once been shipped there directly. The senders’ response moved the perimeter towards the firm. The United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and Japan published common lists of high-priority items — mostly electronic components found in Russian weapons — whose sale to any destination at risk of diversion called for particular scrutiny. The EU’s twelfth package, of December 2023, obliged exporters of the most sensitive goods to write into their contracts with third-country buyers a clause prohibiting re-export to Russia, and in the same month the United States extended its secondary reach to foreign banks serving Russia’s military-industrial base.
The trade statistics show the leak plainly. Figure 10.3 indexes the exports of the 27 member states of the European Union to five of Russia’s neighbours against their 2021 level, as reported by the exporting countries to the IMF (International Monetary Fund 2026). EU exports to Russia fell from 105 billion US dollars in 2021 to 41 billion in 2023. Over the same two years EU exports to Kyrgyzstan rose almost tenfold, from 0.31 to 2.95 billion dollars; exports to Armenia and Kazakhstan more than doubled, and those to Georgia and Uzbekistan rose by more than half (Table 10.2). German exports to Kyrgyzstan, a country of seven million people with no large manufacturing base, went from 59 million dollars to 772 million. Nothing in these economies explains such growth; their position between the European Union and Russia — inside a customs union with Russia, for three of them — does. Maxim Chupilkin, Beata Javorcik and Alexander Plekhanov trace the same “Eurasian roundabout” at the level of products: the surge is concentrated in the goods the European Union stopped sending to Russia directly, and the neighbours’ exports to Russia rose in the same goods (Chupilkin, Javorcik, and Plekhanov 2026).

The numbers also put the leak in proportion. EU exports to the five neighbours rose by 14 billion dollars between 2021 and 2023, while exports to Russia fell by 64 billion: even if every additional dollar had been re-exported, the roundabout replaced about a fifth of the lost trade. The sanctions worked on volume and leaked at the margin — and the margin is where enforcement, and the exporter’s exposure, now sit.
The compliance question is therefore no longer only “is my customer listed?” but “where do my goods end up?”. A manufacturer’s exposure runs through its downstream channels — distributors, resellers, freight forwarders — as well as through its own counterparties.


10.9.3 Secondary sanctions and blocking statutes
Primary sanctions bind the sender’s own nationals and transactions on its territory. Secondary sanctions go further: they threaten third-country firms with penalties — exclusion from the sender’s market, its financial system, or its government contracts — if they deal with the target, even where no person or transaction of the sender is involved.

Secondary sanctions — measures that penalise third-country persons for dealing with a sanctioned target, by restricting their own access to the sender’s market or financial system. They make a sender’s foreign policy binding on firms that are not its nationals, by forcing them to choose between the sender and the target.

The tension this creates between allies is old. When the United States legislated against foreign firms investing in Cuba, Iran and Libya in 1996, the European Union adopted a Blocking Statute forbidding EU firms to comply, and updated it in 2018 when the United States reimposed secondary sanctions on Iran. European firms nevertheless left Iran in large numbers. The choice a secondary sanction forces is not a legal one but a commercial one: the US market and the dollar are worth more to almost any multinational than the target’s market is, and no blocking statute changes that arithmetic. The case of BNP Paribas, which pleaded guilty in the United States in 2014 to processing transactions for sanctioned parties and paid a penalty without precedent at the time, settled the question for many compliance departments: dollar transactions with sanctioned parties anywhere in the world fall within US reach.
The blocking statute has since acquired a mirror image. As Chapter 3 noted, China adopted instruments of its own in 2020 and 2021 against compliance with foreign sanctions it regards as discriminatory, so that a firm large in both the United States and China can find that obeying one state’s law breaches the other’s.


10.9.4 Overcompliance and de-risking
Penalties are severe, rules are complex, lists change without notice, and the cost of a mistake is asymmetric: a bank that refuses a lawful payment loses a fee, a bank that processes an unlawful one may lose its licence. The rational response is to go further than the law.

Overcompliance and de-risking — the withdrawal of firms, and above all banks, from whole countries, sectors or categories of client that the law does not close, because the expected cost of an error exceeds the revenue at stake. The effective scope of sanctions is set by compliance departments as much as by governments.

The evidence that this matters is now substantial. Matthieu Crozet and Julian Hinz, studying the sanctions on Russia after 2014 and the Russian counter-sanctions, find that the trade losses borne by the sending countries fell largely on products that were not embargoed at all — “friendly fire” that they attribute mainly to the financial measures and the uncertainty they created (Crozet and Hinz 2020). A firm selling unrestricted goods to an unrestricted customer may still be unable to get paid, insured or shipped. If its lawyers say the measures do not require it to exit and its bank says it will no longer process payments to that country, its sanctions policy has been set by its bank.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.10 Russia 2022: the exit decision
text:
10.10 Russia 2022: the exit decision
The full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 produced the largest and fastest expansion of sanctions against a major economy since the Second World War, and it confronted hundreds of Western multinationals with a decision most had never modelled: whether to leave a large market that the law, for many of them, did not require them to leave. Public and employee pressure, the difficulty of making payments and moving goods, and the expectation of further measures pushed many to suspend, scale back or exit.
Exit turned out to be harder than announcing it. Russia’s countermeasures made the sale of a foreign-owned business subject to approval by a government commission, required sellers to accept a steep discount on the valuation, and added a payment to the state budget; buyers were frequently local managers or firms close to the state. In 2023 a presidential decree allowed the temporary state management of foreign-owned assets, and the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg were placed under it within weeks. The firms that waited lost the option of selling on their own terms.
The four options — stay, suspend, sell, walk away — each have a cost and a residual risk. McDonald’s sold its Russian restaurants to a local licensee, which reopened them under a new name. Renault sold its controlling stake in AvtoVAZ to a state entity for a symbolic rouble, keeping an option to buy it back within six years — a sale designed to preserve an option on a return. Others suspended operations and paid for idle assets; others stayed, citing obligations to employees or the essential nature of their products, and accepted the reputational cost and the risk of seizure.
The firms that left did not leave a vacuum. Figure 10.4 follows Russia’s imports from its main suppliers, as reported by the exporters. EU exports to Russia, 152 billion dollars in 2013, fell after Crimea, recovered to 105 billion by 2021, and after the invasion fell to 34 billion by 2025. China’s exports to Russia went the other way: from 68 billion dollars in 2021 to 111 billion in 2023 and 116 billion in 2024. Türkiye’s almost doubled, from 5.8 to 10.9 billion, before falling back as Turkish banks, wary of US secondary sanctions, balked at Russian payments. This is Early’s sanctions busting at the scale of a great power: the target found a supplier large enough, and indifferent enough to the senders’ displeasure, to make the measures a cost rather than a constraint (Early 2015).






Figure 10.4: After 2022, China replaced Europe as Russia’s supplier. Exports to Russia by exporter, billions of US dollars. Source: IMF, International Trade in Goods by partner country (IMTS), as reported by the exporter.



For a firm weighing exit, the implication is uncomfortable: its market share was not held in trust. Competitors from non-sending states took it within two years, so a return after sanctions would be a new entry against established rivals — which makes an option to buy back, like Renault’s, worth less than it looks.

The right answer depends on the firm, not on the country. Put the same choice to a consumer-goods firm and to an energy firm, and the answers diverge: the first has brands, local staff and a domestic supply chain that a buyer can run; the second has assets that cannot be moved, partners that may be sanctioned, and a product the target state regards as strategic. Country-level exposure tells a firm that a decision must be taken. It does not tell it which one.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.11 Through which channels sanctions reach the firm
text:
10.11 Through which channels sanctions reach the firm
Sanctions run through all five of the channels set out in Chapter 1. Through market access, export and import bans close markets directly, or indirectly when customers are listed or owned by listed persons, and dual-use export controls close specific product lines to specific end users. Through inputs, a sanctioned supplier can no longer be paid, and the target’s counter-sanctions close supply from the other side, often deeper in the supply chain than the firm can see. Finance and payments is where financial sanctions bite first — the correspondent bank that will not process a payment, the letter of credit that cannot be confirmed, the insurer that will not cover a cargo — and the channel through which overcompliance operates. Through assets and people, assets can be frozen by the sender, or seized, placed under temporary management or sold at a forced discount by the target, and employees are part of the exit’s cost. Through data and operations, software licences, cloud services and technical support may be restricted services in themselves.
Four quantities follow. The firm’s exposure — revenues, assets and suppliers in sanctioned or at-risk jurisdictions — is the starting point. The pipeline of threats is the selection effect applied: the cases that matter most are those not yet imposed. Propagation runs through the banks, insurers and logistics providers whose own exposure could cut the firm off. And the target’s counter-measures against foreign firms on its soil determine, as Russia showed, what an exit costs.

section: 10.12 From episodes to a dataset
text:
10.12 From episodes to a dataset
The Global Sanctions Data Base was built to answer, at scale, questions that case studies cannot: how the use of sanctions has changed over time, what types and objectives dominate, and — joined to trade data — what sanctions do to trade flows (Felbermayr et al. 2020). Its unit is the case: a sanctions episode defined by its senders, its target, its start and end, its types and its objectives, with an outcome coded for each objective. Successive releases have extended the period and revised earlier cases; the third added the measures following the pandemic and the escalating sanctions on Russia (Syropoulos et al. 2024), and the fifth codes 1,794 cases whose first years run from 1949 to 2025; it is distributed on request and for non-commercial use only, so the most complete public record of the instrument cannot be built into a commercial product.
A time series of “active cases” counts, for each year, the episodes whose interval from start to end contains it, and three decisions are buried in that construction. Cases that have not ended must be given an end — and the distributed file gives ongoing cases an end year that is the last year of the data, which is not what its codebook says, so that an analyst who follows the codebook and one who follows the file obtain different series in the final years. A case of several types appears once in each type, so a stacked chart of types overstates the number of cases. And a case is a case whether it consists of a single listing or of a comprehensive embargo, so the number of active cases measures the frequency of the instrument’s use, not its intensity.
The outcome coding carries the success debate into the data. Each objective of each case receives an outcome — total success, partial success, a negotiated settlement, failure, or ongoing — and the share judged successful depends on which objective a multi-objective case is counted under and on whether the ongoing cases, which by definition have not succeeded yet, enter the denominator. These are not technical details. They are Hufbauer’s and Pape’s disagreement reproduced in two lines of arithmetic.
TIES, set beside the GSDB, supplies what the GSDB cannot: the threats that were never imposed. The two differ in unit, period, coding of senders and targets and definition of outcome, so they cannot be merged case by case. What they can do is be compared, year by year, to give an order of magnitude to the selection effect: how much of economic coercion happens before any measure is imposed.
The end-year decision is not peculiar to the GSDB, and TIES shows how much it weighs. Of the 845 TIES cases in which sanctions were imposed, 337 have no end year. Some were still in force when coding stopped; others faded from the news unrecorded. With the date of the last news story the coders found, an analyst has three defensible rules: the case was still in force at the end of the data, it ended at the last news report, or — the implicit choice of anyone who drops missing values — it lasted only the year it began. Figure 10.5 draws the number of imposed sanctions in force each year under each rule. Until the late 1980s the three series barely differ. After 1990 they part company: in 2000 the count is 369 under the first rule, 91 under the second and 59 under the third; under the first it rises to a peak of 412 in 2003, under the other two it peaks in 1993 and then declines. Whether sanctions kept multiplying after the sanctions decade depends on a line of code the reader of the chart never sees.






Figure 10.5: How many sanctions were in force? It depends on how open cases are closed. Imposed TIES cases in force each year, under three rules for the 337 cases without an end year. Source: Morgan, Bapat and Kobayashi, TIES v4.0.



The record also says who uses the instrument (Table 10.3). The United States is the primary sender in 681 of the 1,412 cases — 48 percent, about half in every decade but the 1970s. Less often noticed is the list of targets: the United States itself comes first, followed by Japan, South Korea, China, the European Community and Canada. In this record, economic coercion is largely a tool used among trading partners, many of them allies, over trade.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.13 A short review of the literature
text:
10.13 A short review of the literature

The empirical study of sanctions begins with Hufbauer et al. (2007), whose three editions established the case list, the two-component coding of success and the “about a third” finding; Pape (1997) audited the claimed successes and found few that survived, Elliott (1998) replied, and Pape (1998) rejoined. Baldwin (1985) had already argued that effectiveness must be judged relative to the alternatives and their costs, which reframes the whole exchange. The mechanism literature runs from Galtung (1967), whose study of Rhodesia dismantled the “naive theory” that pain produces compliance, to Kirshner (1997), who located the effect of sanctions in the redistribution of power among groups within the target.
The strategic turn came with Drezner (1999), who explained why sanctions are imposed most on the adversaries least likely to concede, and Drezner (2003), who identified the selection effect of threats. The data response was TIES, which records threats as well as impositions (Morgan, Bapat, and Krustev 2009; Morgan, Bapat, and Kobayashi 2014); its outcome codes show complete acquiescence more often at the threat stage than after imposition, above all in economic disputes. Early (2015) showed how third-country sanctions busters sustain targets, which helps explain why multilateral sanctions do not always outperform unilateral ones.
On design, Biersteker, Eckert, and Tourinho (2016) evaluate UN targeted sanctions against the purposes of coercing, constraining and signalling, and Peksen (2009) documents the human-rights cost of sanctions to the populations of target states. Farrell and Newman (2019) explain the rise of financial sanctions through the chokepoints of global networks. The GSDB (Felbermayr et al. 2020) and its later releases (Syropoulos et al. 2024) made it possible to study sanctions at the scale of trade data, and Crozet and Hinz (2020) used that kind of data to show that much of the trade cost of the Russia sanctions after 2014 fell on products that were not sanctioned at all — the quantitative trace of overcompliance. Chupilkin, Javorcik, and Plekhanov (2026) trace the opposite leak after 2022: goods rerouted to Russia through the Caucasus and Central Asia.

title: 10  Economic Sanctions: Do They Work, and Whom Do They Hit?
section: 10.14 What the case count does not license
text:
10.14 What the case count does not license
The descriptive record of the GSDB is clear in its broad lines: the number of active sanctions cases has risen steeply since the end of the Cold War, and the mix of instruments has shifted from trade towards finance, travel and named persons. That picture is the right starting point for any view of sanctions risk. It is also easy to over-read, and four conclusions often drawn from it are not supported.
It does not license a conclusion about a firm’s exposure: a count of cases naming a country says how often senders have used the instrument against it, not how much of a firm’s revenue, supply or payments the measures touch, and a single financial sanction on a country’s largest banks can matter more than a dozen travel bans. It does not license a conclusion about the perimeter, which is drawn by ownership rules, secondary sanctions, diversion clauses and the firm’s own banks, and which reaches customers in countries that appear nowhere in the data as targets. It does not license a conclusion about the pipeline, because the cases that would matter most next year are threats today. And it says nothing about duration: whether a given set of measures will be lifted soon enough to make waiting the cheaper option, a cost the Russian exits showed to be set less by the senders than by the target’s countermeasures.
The deeper conclusion is about the instrument itself. Sanctions were designed to regulate conflict between states without war, and on the evidence they do that job partially, at a cost that falls largely on people who did not choose the policy. For firms the balance is less ambiguous. Each expansion of the instrument — from trade to finance, from lists to ownership, from targets to the neighbours through which goods are diverted — has moved more of the work of enforcement onto the private sector. Whatever sanctions do to their targets, they have made the multinational the place where foreign policy is executed, and its sanctions risk lives in its footprint, its counterparties’ owners, its banks, its distributors and the countermeasures of its host states. None of those is in the case list.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
text:
11.1 Infrastructure overhead
Few multinationals own a satellite. Almost all of them depend on one, and most do not know which. A container line tracks its ships by satellite and talks to their crews by satellite when they are out of range of land. A mining company runs its remote sites over satellite links. An agribusiness forecasts harvests from imagery, an insurer settles flood claims from it, and a buyer of commodities checks the stockpiles of its suppliers with it. Above all, almost every firm depends on satellites for time. Telecommunications networks, electricity grids, data centres and trading venues synchronise their clocks to the signals of global navigation satellite systems, because those signals carry time from atomic clocks in orbit to any receiver on the ground, cheaply and everywhere.
Three services carry most of this dependence. Positioning, navigation and timing comes from four global systems, each run by a state: GPS by the United States, Galileo by the European Union, BeiDou by China and GLONASS by Russia. Connectivity comes from operators in geostationary orbit, 36,000 kilometres up, and since 2019 from constellations of thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit, a few hundred kilometres up. Earth observation comes from state agencies and from a growing number of commercial imaging firms.
Chapters 8 and 10 showed how networks become instruments of power: a network’s hubs are under someone’s jurisdiction, and whoever has jurisdiction can watch the traffic or cut it off. The network of this chapter is physically above the firm. Its hubs are a handful of states and, increasingly, a handful of companies, and its environment is degrading in a way no terrestrial network’s does — through debris that stays where it was created for years or centuries. The scale of the change is recent. The European Space Agency’s 2026 environment report notes that the exponential growth in the number of new payloads continued in 2025, driven by a higher launch frequency, rideshare launches and the deployment of large constellations by commercial operators (ESA Space Debris Office 2026).
The question of this chapter is who holds the risk when orbit is crowded, contested and dominated by one operator — and what the firm can do about it. The answer it develops is that the firm holds more of it than it thinks, that most of it arrives through the reversible and unspectacular threats rather than the destructive ones, and that dependence on a satellite service is, by the construction of space law, dependence on a state.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.2 A domain written for two superpowers
text:
11.2 A domain written for two superpowers
The law of outer space was written at speed, during the Cold War, by and for two states that were then the only ones able to get there. Sputnik’s launch in October 1957 settled one question before anyone had negotiated it: the Soviet satellite passed over every country on Earth, and no state protested that its airspace had been violated. The principle that satellites may overfly territory — which the United States, planning reconnaissance satellites of its own, had every interest in establishing — became the foundation of the domain.
The rest of the foundation was laid in the Outer Space Treaty, opened for signature in January 1967 and in force by October of that year (United Nations 1967). It remains the constitution of the domain, and the articles that matter to a firm can be read in two pages. Article II declares that outer space “is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means”: no one can own an orbit. Article IV forbids placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, and reserves the Moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes — but it says nothing to prohibit conventional weapons in orbit, or the testing of weapons that destroy satellites from the ground. Article VI makes states internationally responsible for national activities in space “whether such activities are carried on by governmental agencies or by non-governmental entities”, and requires those activities to be authorised and continually supervised by “the appropriate State”. Article VII makes the launching state liable for damage caused by its objects. Article IX requires states to act with “due regard” to the interests of others and to consult before activities that could cause harmful interference — the closest the Treaty comes to traffic rules, without anyone to enforce them.

Orbital commons — Earth orbit treated as a resource that no one may appropriate (Outer Space Treaty, Article II) and from whose use no one can easily be excluded, but whose use by one actor degrades it for others — through congestion of orbits and spectrum and through debris. The commons is legal in origin and physical in its consequences.

Article IV’s silence on conventional weapons was not an accident; neither superpower wanted to give up the option. Its prohibition on nuclear weapons in orbit, by contrast, had been learned the hard way.

From the archive · Starfish Prime, 1962
On 9 July 1962 the United States detonated a thermonuclear warhead of about 1.4 megatons some 400 kilometres above Johnston Island in the Pacific. The test, Starfish Prime, was intended to study the effects of a nuclear explosion at high altitude. Its most lasting effect was one its planners had underestimated: electrons from the explosion were trapped in the Earth’s magnetic field, creating an artificial radiation belt that persisted for years.
The satellites then in low orbit were few, and several were damaged. Telstar 1, the first commercial communications satellite — built by AT&T’s Bell Laboratories and launched the day after the test — suffered radiation damage to its electronics and failed within months; Britain’s first satellite, Ariel 1, was also damaged. A single test by one state had degraded an orbital environment shared by everyone, and the first commercial satellite was among the casualties.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in outer space, and the Outer Space Treaty four years later prohibited nuclear weapons in orbit. Neither prohibited the next form of the same problem: a conventional weapon that destroys a satellite and fills its orbit with fragments.

Article II has also become the ground of a newer contest, over resources rather than weapons. The Treaty forbids national appropriation of outer space and celestial bodies; it does not say whether a firm may own what it extracts from them. The United States answered the question for its own citizens in the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015, which recognises their property rights in resources obtained from asteroids and other bodies, and Luxembourg followed with a law of its own in 2017. In 2020 the United States and seven partners signed the Artemis Accords, a non-binding set of principles for the civil exploration of the Moon that treat resource extraction as consistent with the Treaty; China and Russia announced a joint lunar research station the following year and gathered partners of their own. The pattern resembles the contest over technical standards described in Chapter 6: where the treaty process has stalled, rules are written by coalitions, and a firm’s access to a future market depends on which coalition its home state has joined.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.3 Liability, registration and the right to transmit
text:
11.3 Liability, registration and the right to transmit
The Outer Space Treaty is the constitution; three further layers turn it into rules a firm encounters.
The first is liability and registration. The Liability Convention of 1972 elaborated Article VII: a launching state is absolutely liable for damage its space objects cause on the surface of the Earth or to aircraft in flight, and liable for fault for damage elsewhere in space. The Registration Convention of 1975 requires launching states to register their objects with the United Nations. The two together mean that every object in orbit has, in law, a state that answers for it — long after it has stopped working.

From the archive · Cosmos 954, 1978
On 24 January 1978 a Soviet ocean-surveillance satellite, Cosmos 954, re-entered the atmosphere over the Northwest Territories of Canada. It was powered by a small nuclear reactor, and its re-entry scattered radioactive debris over a wide stretch of the Canadian north. Canada and the United States mounted a search and clean-up operation, Operation Morning Light, that lasted for months.
Canada presented a claim to the Soviet Union under the Liability Convention and general principles of international law, for the cost of locating, recovering and cleaning up the debris. The claim was settled in 1981, by protocol, for three million Canadian dollars — about half the amount claimed. It remains the only claim ever brought under the Convention.
The case shows both the strength and the limits of the regime. Liability attaches to a state, and a state paid. But it took three years, the settlement was negotiated rather than adjudicated, and the claimant was a state. A firm whose satellite is destroyed by a fragment from another state’s anti-satellite test has no standing under the Convention: it must persuade its own state to claim, against a launching state that may deny responsibility, for damage whose cause it may be unable to prove.

The second layer is spectrum. A satellite is useless without radio frequencies to command it and to carry its service, and frequencies and orbital positions are coordinated by the International Telecommunication Union through its Radio Regulations. An operator’s state files a satellite network with the ITU and must coordinate it with networks filed earlier, so priority goes, broadly, to the first to file. The incentive is to file early and large — sometimes for “paper satellites” that may never fly — and the result is that orbital slots and frequencies are a scarce asset allocated by a procedure most firms never see.
The third layer is national licensing. Article VI’s “authorization and continuing supervision” becomes, in practice, a set of permits: to launch, to use spectrum, to operate a remote-sensing system, to export a satellite or its components, to land a service in a national market. This is where a firm meets space law directly, and where the balance of power enters most visibly — through the export-control lists discussed below and through decisions about which foreign constellations may sell service in which countries. It is also where the rules on debris acquire teeth. The international guidelines are voluntary, but a licence condition is not: in 2022 the US Federal Communications Commission adopted a rule requiring operators of satellites in low orbit that it licenses, or that serve the US market, to dispose of them within five years of the end of their missions, replacing a guideline of twenty-five years. A firm’s satellite provider is therefore bound not by one law of space but by the licensing conditions of every state whose market it serves.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.4 The physics of a commons
text:
11.4 The physics of a commons
Law makes orbit a commons in one sense: no one may own it. Physics makes it a commons in the stricter sense economists use. A common-pool resource is one from which exclusion is difficult and whose use by one actor subtracts from what is left for others. Garrett Hardin’s parable of the herdsmen on a common pasture, each adding animals because he captures the whole gain while bearing only a share of the cost, is the classic statement of why such resources tend to be overused (Hardin 1968). Elinor Ostrom showed that real communities often escape the tragedy through rules they design and enforce themselves — but under conditions of clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions that Earth orbit does not meet (Ostrom 1990). Brian Weeden and Tiffany Chow applied her framework to space and found most of its design principles missing (Weeden and Chow 2012).
What turns congestion into a tragedy in orbit is a mechanism identified by Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais in 1978 (Kessler and Cour-Palais 1978). Objects in the same orbital shell occasionally collide; each collision produces fragments; the fragments raise the density of objects in the shell and therefore the rate of further collisions. Below a critical density, the atmosphere drags enough debris down to keep the population in check. Above it, collisions generate fragments faster than drag removes them, and the debris population grows on its own.

Kessler syndrome — the self-sustaining growth of the debris population in an orbital shell once the density of objects passes a threshold at which collisions create fragments faster than atmospheric drag removes them. Past the threshold, the population grows even if nobody launches again.

Altitude matters enormously, because the drag that cleans orbits weakens with height. Debris a few hundred kilometres up re-enters within years; debris above about 800 kilometres can remain for decades or centuries. A fragmentation in a high, busy shell is therefore a long-lived degradation of an asset shared by every operator in it. Two decades ago, simulations by NASA’s debris specialists already suggested that the low-orbit debris population would keep growing through collisions even if all launches stopped (Liou and Johnson 2006).
The public catalogue shows where the objects are today (Figure 11.1). Of the 35,036 catalogued objects in Earth orbit in the October 2026 vintage used here, 29,200 have a mean altitude between 200 and 2,000 kilometres. Below 600 kilometres there are 14,568, and 95 percent of them are payloads — 11,153 of them Starlink satellites, stacked in a few narrow shells around 350, 480 and 550 kilometres. Between 700 and 900 kilometres the picture inverts: of 5,665 objects, only 12 percent are payloads, and the rest are debris and spent rocket stages, many of them left by the events described below. The two populations sit in different places for the reason Kessler gave. Operators of large constellations fly low so that a failed satellite re-enters within a few years; the fragments of explosions and tests above 700 kilometres stay where they were made.






Figure 11.1: Satellites crowd below 600 km; debris lingers higher, where drag is weak. Catalogued objects in Earth orbit by mean altitude, in 25-kilometre bands. Source: CelesTrak SATCAT, October 2026 vintage.



For a firm the chart says that “orbit” is not one asset but several. The low shells, where the new broadband constellations fly, are crowded with working satellites that manoeuvre and are cleaned by drag; the risk there is congestion and the conduct of a few large operators. The shells near 800 kilometres, used by Earth-observation and weather satellites, carry the legacy of the twentieth century’s tests and explosions, and that legacy will be there for decades whatever anyone does next.
Economists have since modelled the incentives. Nodir Adilov, Peter Alexander and Brendan Cunningham show that, because each operator ignores the collision risk its satellites and debris impose on others, open access leads to more launches and more debris than would be efficient (Adilov, Alexander, and Cunningham 2015). Akhil Rao, Matthew Burgess and Daniel Kaffine estimate that an internationally harmonised fee on each satellite in orbit — making operators pay for the risk they impose — would greatly increase the long-run value of the space industry (Rao, Burgess, and Kaffine 2020). No such fee exists. Mitigation guidelines adopted through the UN and by space agencies ask operators to limit debris and to remove satellites from busy orbits at the end of their lives; compliance is voluntary and uneven.

For the firm: an orbit is a shared infrastructure whose quality is set by its least careful user. A destructive test by one state, or a rocket stage that explodes years after launch, raises the collision risk — and the insurance price — for every operator in that shell, and therefore for every customer of those operators.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.5 Three readings of the new space race
text:
11.5 Three readings of the new space race
Who will govern this commons, and in whose interest? International relations offers three readings of what has come to be called the new space race, and they do not exclude one another.
The first is classical geopolitics carried upwards. Everett Dolman’s Astropolitik takes Mackinder’s logic — whoever controls the pivot controls the world — and applies it to orbit: whoever controls low Earth orbit controls access to the rest of space, and through it can dominate the Earth below (Dolman 2002). On this realist reading the United States should seize and hold that control while it can, and space is a territory to dominate, its orbits and transfer routes the chokepoints of a new strategic geography. It is the anarchy of Chapter 3, with orbits in place of straits.
The second reading is institutional and commercial. Saadia Pekkanen describes the new space race as driven by three intertwined trends (Pekkanen 2019). Democratisation: many more states, and many non-state actors, now operate in space. Commercialisation: firms no longer only supply governments but strike out on their own, with their own capital and customers. Militarisation: states increasingly treat space as a domain of warfare. Binding them together is the fact that about 95 percent of space technologies, on her account, are dual-use. With treaty-making in decline, the domain is governed less by new international law than by national legislation, contracts, and a few old principles. On this reading space is a market, and the firms in it are part of the security problem.
The third reading puts the Earth back at the centre. Bleddyn Bowen argues that spacepower matters for its effects on Earth: orbit is a “cosmic coastline” from which states support — and threaten — what happens on land, at sea and in the air (Bowen 2020). Satellites are valuable because they make terrestrial forces see, communicate and navigate; that is also why they are targets when terrestrial power is contested.
Read together, the three explain why the same constellation can be a consumer broadband business, a military communications network and an instrument of foreign policy all at once. Pekkanen supplies the dual use; Dolman and Bowen supply the strategic stakes. For a multinational the practical conclusion is the same under all three: a commercial satellite service is never only commercial.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.6 Counterspace: what states can do to satellites
text:
11.6 Counterspace: what states can do to satellites
If satellites are targets, the question is what can be done to them, by whom, and with what consequences for the firms that use them. The Secure World Foundation’s annual open-source assessment tracks the capabilities of thirteen countries to deceive, disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space systems, in five categories (Samson and Brett 2026).

Counterspace capabilities — the means of deceiving, disrupting, denying, degrading or destroying space systems: direct-ascent missiles, co-orbital systems, electronic warfare, directed energy and cyber operations. They differ in whether their effects are reversible and in who bears them first — the satellite’s owner, every operator in the orbit, or the users on the ground.

Direct-ascent weapons are missiles launched from the Earth to destroy a satellite. Their effects are irreversible and, at most altitudes, create debris that threatens every operator in the shell. Co-orbital systems are satellites that approach another to inspect it, interfere with it or attack it. Electronic warfare jams or spoofs signals — the uplink to a satellite, its downlink to users, or navigation signals on the ground — and its effects end when the jamming stops. Directed-energy weapons use lasers or microwaves to dazzle or damage sensors. Cyber operations attack satellites, ground stations or user terminals, and can disable a service without touching a satellite.
The assessment’s central finding is the one that matters most for business: many states have researched and tested destructive capabilities, but only non-destructive ones are actively used against satellites in current military operations. Four states have destroyed one of their own satellites with a missile launched from the ground: the United States in 1985 — and, in 2008, by intercepting a failing satellite at low altitude — China in 2007, India in 2019 and Russia in 2021. In April 2022 the United States declared that it would not conduct destructive direct-ascent tests, and in December 2022 the UN General Assembly called on all states to make the same commitment.
What firms have actually suffered is the reversible kind. On 24 February 2022, the day Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, a cyberattack on the ground segment of Viasat’s KA-SAT network disabled thousands of user modems in Ukraine and across Europe, including those used for the remote monitoring of wind farms in central Europe. The European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States attributed the attack to Russia (UK Government 2022). The satellite was untouched; the service failed for its customers, many of them nowhere near the war. Since then, the jamming and spoofing of navigation signals around conflict zones has become routine. In 2024 Finnair suspended its flights to Tartu, in Estonia, for several weeks because interference made the airport’s satellite-based approach procedures unusable.

The lesson for an analyst. Destructive tests make headlines and debris. Jamming, spoofing and cyberattacks on ground segments make losses — and the losses fall on the customers, not on the satellite. A firm’s counterspace exposure is measured on the ground, in the regions where its ships, aircraft and sites depend on signals from orbit.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.7 The debris record, and how it is counted
text:
11.7 The debris record, and how it is counted
The most complete public account of the orbital environment comes from ESA’s Space Debris Office, which has published an annual Space Environment Report since 2017. The 2026 edition, with data to the end of 2025, is the source of the figures that follow (ESA Space Debris Office 2026), and its method deserves reading before its numbers.
ESA counts two kinds of objects. Catalogued objects are those tracked and published in catalogues: the US public catalogue, the Russian Vimpel catalogue and, for the early decades, the United Kingdom’s historical RAE tables. Asserted objects are known to exist by design — a satellite released from a dispenser, a component separated as planned — even if not yet catalogued. The two are cross-correlated in ESA’s DISCOS database and classified into object classes. Objects too small or too erratic to be tracked are outside the report’s scope.
On that basis, the report counts 44,964 objects in Earth orbit at the end of 2025, of which 16,946 are payloads, and 25,060 objects in low Earth orbit (ESA Space Debris Office 2026). It observes that, ever since the start of the space age, there has been more debris in orbit than operational satellites. And its most important finding for anyone who thinks the debris problem is the weapons tests is this: fragmentations other than collisions — explosions, mostly of old rocket stages and batteries — are the dominant source of debris. Non-deliberate fragmentations have averaged 9.8 a year over the last two decades, and 2024 alone added more than 3,000 catalogued fragments, mostly from propulsion-related break-ups.
The report’s count of objects in geocentric orbit by object class since 1957 shows the cumulative result of seven decades of launches, explosions, collisions and re-entries, and three events stand out on it. On 11 January 2007 China destroyed its Fengyun-1C weather satellite with a ground-launched missile, at about 850 kilometres; the test remains the largest single source of catalogued debris in the public catalogue, and most of its thousands of fragments are still in orbit. On 10 February 2009 the active Iridium 33 and the defunct Cosmos 2251 collided at about 780 kilometres — the first accidental collision between two intact satellites, Kessler’s mechanism observed. And on 15 November 2021 Russia destroyed Cosmos 1408 at roughly 470 to 490 kilometres, producing some 1,800 catalogued fragments; at that altitude almost all re-entered within three years, and ESA attributes the 2022 spike in re-entering debris to the test.
The contrast between the first and third events is a lesson in altitude. Both were deliberate destructions of a satellite by its own state; one polluted a high orbit for decades, the other a low orbit for a few years. A count of objects treats them alike.
The public catalogue lets the lesson be put in numbers, because every fragment is named after its parent. Table 11.1 counts the catalogued fragments of the main destructive tests and of three accidental break-ups, and how many of them are still in orbit. Of the 3,531 catalogued fragments of Fengyun-1C, 2,311 — almost two in three — are still in orbit nearly two decades later, at a median altitude of about 830 kilometres. Of the 1,806 fragments of Cosmos 1408, four remain. The American intercept of 2008 and India’s test of 2019, both conducted at low altitude, have left nothing in the catalogue. The 2009 collision sits between the two: a third of the Cosmos 2251 fragments and a fifth of the Iridium 33 fragments are still up.

The last three rows support ESA’s finding that accidental fragmentations, not weapons, are the larger source of debris. Two ageing American weather satellites and one military weather satellite, each of which broke up years after its mission ended — the DMSP satellite through a battery failure — together left 526 fragments still in orbit between 700 and 800 kilometres, not far short of the 723 left by the 2009 collision. None of these break-ups made headlines; each degraded a shell that other operators use.

What the count does not measure. It counts objects, not risk: a ten-centimetre fragment and a five-tonne rocket stage each count once, and the objects too small to catalogue — the majority of the fragments able to disable a satellite — do not appear at all. It is drawn from catalogues that themselves improve: when sensors get better, the count rises with nothing new having happened in orbit. And it shows the environment, not the exposure of any operator or customer, which depends on which shells their satellites use.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.8 From a catalogue to a stock
text:
11.8 From a catalogue to a stock
ESA’s series can be approximated from public data, and the approximation shows how a concept — the number of objects in orbit — becomes a number. The public catalogue, maintained from US Space Force data and redistributed by CelesTrak, does not record a stock. It records objects: one row for each catalogued object over its whole life, with a launch date and, if it has re-entered, a decay date. There is no “year” in the file. An object is in orbit in a given year if it was launched by then and had not decayed by then, so the stock in each year is the running sum of launches minus the running sum of decays — a stock rebuilt from two flows. Much of what a risk analyst needs to know is a stock of this kind, which no one publishes and which has to be rebuilt from the events that change it.
The construction exposes the catalogue’s decisions. Debris carries the launch date of its parent object, not the date of the event that created it: the fragments of China’s 2007 test are dated to the launch of Fengyun-1C in 1999, so a debris series built on launch dates moves in the wrong year, and the published record and the reconstruction disagree precisely at the events that matter. “Not decayed” is not the same as “in Earth orbit”, because some objects orbit the Sun, the Moon or a Lagrange point. The owner field records a country, organisation or company code, not the operator: every Starlink satellite is simply American, and the former Soviet Union and Russia share one code. Operational status describes today only, so the file cannot say how many satellites were active in any past year. And the public catalogue is not the environment: it omits classified objects and everything too small to track, which is one reason ESA’s totals, drawn from more catalogues and asserted objects, are higher.
The dating decision can be measured, because a second public catalogue records what the first does not. Jonathan McDowell’s General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects gives each fragment the date on which it separated from its parent as well as the parent’s launch date (McDowell 2026). Figure 11.2 rebuilds the stock of objects in Earth orbit at the end of each year from that catalogue, with debris dated by the event that created it, and sets beside it the total obtained from CelesTrak’s copy of the public catalogue (Kelso 2026) with debris dated by its parent’s launch. The two agree on payloads and rocket bodies and disagree, sometimes by a factor of two, on debris. Dated by launch, the debris in orbit at the end of 2000 numbers 16,843 objects, because every fragment ever created from a satellite launched by then — including those of the 2007 test, the 2009 collision and every later break-up — is counted as if it already existed. Dated by the event, it numbers 6,530. The launch-dated series barely moves in 2007 (it rises by 39 objects) because the Fengyun-1C fragments were already in it from 1999; the event-dated series jumps by 3,765. The two series converge only after 2021, once most backdated fragments have either been created or re-entered.






Figure 11.2: Debris built the orbital population; payloads overtook it in 2024. Catalogued objects in Earth orbit at the end of each year, with debris dated by the event that created it; the dashed line dates debris by its parent’s launch. Source: GCAT (J. C. McDowell); CelesTrak SATCAT.



The event-dated series also shows the turn of the last few years. Debris outnumbered payloads in the catalogue from the 1960s onwards, as ESA notes. At the end of 2025 the reconstruction counts 16,899 payloads, 2,015 rocket bodies and 12,812 pieces of debris; payloads first outnumbered debris in 2024. The crossing is not a sign that the debris problem is solving itself. It is the arrival of the large constellations, whose satellites are counted as payloads while they work and after they fail, and the slow re-entry of the low fragments of the 2021 test.

Its count of payloads is close to the reconstructions’, so the difference is almost entirely debris: the environment a firm’s satellite provider actually faces is more crowded than any public download shows.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.9 One operator
text:
11.9 One operator
The new space race has a feature the Cold War one did not. In the first years of the space age, concentration was extreme because only two states could launch anything; it fell for decades as Europe, Japan, China, India and many others acquired the capability, and as commercial operators multiplied. It has risen again — not because states have dropped out, but because one company has launched more satellites than everyone else together. SpaceX’s Starlink, first launched in May 2019, grew in six years into the majority of the world’s operating satellites. Measured on the public catalogue’s owner codes, the concentration of payloads launched each year has returned to levels last seen in the Cold War, with a firm rather than a superpower at the top.
Concentration needs a measure, and the standard one is the index that antitrust authorities use. Its origins are in geopolitics: Albert Hirschman devised an index of the concentration of a country’s trade in 1945, to show how Nazi Germany had used the structure of trade to make its smaller partners dependent on it (Hirschman 1945). Orris Herfindahl reinvented it a few years later for industrial concentration, and it carries both their names.

Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) — the sum of the squared market shares of all participants, with shares in percent, so that it runs from near 0 (many small participants) to 10,000 (one participant with everything). It weights large shares heavily: one participant with 75 percent contributes 5,625 on its own. US merger guidelines treat markets above 2,500 (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2010) or, in the 2023 revision, above 1,800 (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2023) as highly concentrated.

The index, built from the catalogue, inherits the catalogue’s owner-code problem twice over. Concentration by state hides the fact that one company dominates the American share; concentration by operator must be reconstructed from object names. Each choice yields a different index, and each answers a different question — about the balance of power among states, or about the dependence of customers on firms.
Figure 11.3 shows where the concentration comes from. In 2018, 448 payloads were launched, two of them SpaceX’s. In 2020 the total was 1,242 and 833 were SpaceX’s; in 2025 it was 4,495, of which 3,169 — 71 percent — were SpaceX’s. China launched 368 payloads in 2025, Russia 88, and every other American operator together 530. The rest of the world, Europe, Japan and India included, launched 340.






Figure 11.3: One company now launches most of the world’s satellites. Payloads by launch year, grouped by operator (SpaceX) and owner state. Source: GCAT (J. C. McDowell).



Figure 11.4 computes the index on payloads launched each year, by owner state and by operator, from the GCAT codes. By state, the index stood at 7,450 in 1960 and 7,898 in 1980, when the Soviet Union launched most of the world’s satellites; it fell to 2,559 in 2000 and a low of 1,312 in 2008, as Europe, China, India, Japan and many smaller states entered. Since 2019 it has risen again, to 6,845 in 2025 — Cold War levels — because the American share has grown with one firm. By operator, the index was below 1,000 for most of the space age, and as low as 142 in 2013, because even the Soviet programme was spread across many agencies and design bureaus; it reached 4,589 in 2020 and 5,007 in 2025. The two lines tell different stories about the past and the same one about the present. The balance among states looks like the 1980s; the balance among operators has no precedent.






Figure 11.4: Concentration of new satellites is back at Cold War levels, with a firm on top. Herfindahl–Hirschman index of payloads launched each year, by owner state and by operator. Source: GCAT (J. C. McDowell).



Flows are not stocks, and launches overstate the weight of a constellation whose satellites last five years against geostationary satellites that last fifteen. On the stock, the conclusion is the same. Of the 17,247 catalogued objects marked as operational in the October 2026 vintage of the public catalogue, 11,151 — 65 percent — are Starlink satellites.
Concentration matters to a firm because of what it implies about dependence, and Starlink in Ukraine shows what that dependence means. Within days of the 2022 invasion, Starlink terminals became a backbone of Ukraine’s military and civil communications. The company’s decisions about where its service would work — including, by its owner’s account, a refusal to enable it for an attack near Crimea in 2022 — became questions of war policy, and governments moved to contract for the service directly.
Farrell and Newman’s framework, introduced in Chapter 8, applies without modification (Farrell and Newman 2019). A constellation is a hub. Its operator sees who connects and from where — a panopticon — and can switch off a user, a region or a country — a chokepoint. Weaponisation requires two conditions: that the network be concentrated, and that a state can direct the firm that runs the hub. Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty guarantees the second, because every operator has a licensing state that is internationally responsible for its activities and must supervise them. A firm that depends on one operator depends on that operator’s state as well.
States are responding as the balance-of-power reasoning of Chapter 3 would predict: by building their own. The European Union’s IRIS² secure-connectivity programme, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/588, China’s Qianfan and Guowang constellations, and the many national launch programmes are all, in part, answers to dependence on one American firm. Export controls draw the same line from the other side. Spacecraft and their components sit either on the US Munitions List, under Category XV of the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or — for most commercial satellites since 2014 — under the Export Administration Regulations, in the “9x515” entries; a non-US manufacturer whose satellite contains a controlled US component needs US permission to sell it to some customers. The balance of power reaches into the bill of materials.
Navigation is the older case of the same pattern, and the one on which almost every firm already depends. GPS was built by the US military. Its opening to the world followed a tragedy: after the Soviet Union shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, which had strayed into Soviet airspace, in September 1983, the United States announced that GPS would be made available for civilian use once it was operational. For years the civilian signal was deliberately degraded — “Selective Availability” — until the degradation was switched off in May 2000. The service on which the world’s networks and logistics came to rely was, and remains, a gift that one state chose to give and could in principle withdraw or degrade, regionally or globally. Europe’s decision to build Galileo, and China’s to build BeiDou, were in large part refusals to accept that dependence. For a firm, the existence of four global systems is a genuine diversification — but only if its receivers use more than one, and only against the failure or withdrawal of a system, not against a jammer in the next port.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.10 Through which channels, and what the firm can do
text:
11.10 Through which channels, and what the firm can do
Space risk reaches the profit and loss account through the same five channels as every other risk in this book, and naming the channel is the first step towards a decision.
Through market access, export controls and licensing decide whether a satellite, a terminal or a service can be sold or switched on in a given market, and spectrum and landing rights decide whether a constellation may serve a country at all. Through inputs, a firm that buys connectivity for its ships or mines from one constellation, or that times its networks from one state’s navigation system, has a single point of failure with a sovereign behind it. Through finance and payments, trading venues and payment systems time-stamp transactions from navigation signals, and the insurance capacity for space assets — a thin market — shrinks after large losses. Through assets and people, ships and aircraft operating in jammed or spoofed regions are rerouted, delayed, or misreport their positions, with consequences for safety and for sanctions compliance alike. Through data and operations, a cyberattack on a ground segment cuts the firm’s links, as the KA-SAT modems showed, and the loss of an imagery feed leaves a crop forecast or a supply-chain monitor blind.
Four kinds of evidence bear on that exposure, and each can be tied in advance to a decision. Dependence: the share of a critical service — connectivity, imagery, timing — supplied by one operator or one state’s system; above a share the firm has fixed beforehand, the decision is to contract a second. Interference: the official warnings of navigation-signal interference that aviation authorities publish for the regions where the firm’s ships, aircraft or sites operate. Environment: destructive tests and fragmentation events in the orbital shells its providers use, and the yearly indicators in ESA’s report. Rules: changes in export-control lists, licensing conditions and ITU filings that affect its suppliers or markets.
The strategies available each have a cost and a limit. A firm can buy multi-orbit, multi-operator connectivity — geostationary and low-orbit links from two providers — at the price of integration, but the second operator may share the first one’s licensing state. It can use multi-constellation receivers that combine GPS, Galileo and others, which is cheap and protects against the failure of one system, but a local jammer can still blind them all. It can invest in terrestrial back-ups — holdover clocks and time delivered over fibre and cellular networks — which requires capital and is unavailable at sea or at remote sites. It can buy insurance, in a thin market whose capacity shrinks after large losses. And it can practise compliance by design, classifying every space-related component it buys or sells under the relevant export-control regimes, at the cost of staff and delay, knowing that the rules change with the balance of power.
A single case ties these together. A shipping subsidiary’s only broadband at sea is one low-orbit constellation; the operator’s government has been asked by an ally to switch the service off over a strait the firm’s ships use. The firm’s options this quarter turn on the distinction between dependence on a service and dependence on a state. A second operator under the same licensing state diversifies the first and not the second; a second operator under another state diversifies both, at the price of a second set of export controls and a second government’s discretion.

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.11 A short review of the literature
text:
11.11 A short review of the literature

The legal foundation is the Outer Space Treaty (United Nations 1967), whose Articles II, VI and VII make orbit unappropriable, place every private operator under a responsible state, and attach liability to the launching state. The governance problem it leaves open is that of a commons. Hardin (1968) states why open-access resources are overused and Ostrom (1990) the conditions under which communities escape the tragedy; Weeden and Chow (2012) apply Ostrom’s design principles to orbit and find most of them absent. The physical mechanism is Kessler and Cour-Palais (1978), with Liou and Johnson (2006) showing by simulation that the low-orbit debris population would grow even without new launches. The economics of the externality is set out by Adilov, Alexander, and Cunningham (2015), and Rao, Burgess, and Kaffine (2020) estimate the gains from orbital-use fees.
The strategic literature divides along the lines of this chapter’s three readings. Dolman (2002) carries classical geopolitics into orbit; Bowen (2020) argues that spacepower matters for its terrestrial effects; Pekkanen (2019) describes the democratisation, commercialisation and militarisation of a domain in which most technology is dual-use and treaty-making has stalled. The empirical record of threats is the Secure World Foundation’s annual assessment (Samson and Brett 2026), and that of the environment ESA’s annual report (ESA Space Debris Office 2026); the public catalogue redistributed by CelesTrak (Kelso 2026) and McDowell’s GCAT (McDowell 2026), which dates each fragment by the event that created it, allow the record to be rebuilt and its dating decisions tested.
For the firm, the bridge is Farrell and Newman (2019): a concentrated constellation under a state’s jurisdiction meets both conditions for weaponised interdependence. The measure of concentration is Hirschman (1945)’s index, conceived to analyse how trade structures create political dependence, and its antitrust thresholds are those of the US merger guidelines (U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission 2010, 2023).

title: 11  Space Geopolitics: The Orbital Commons and the New Space Race
section: 11.12 What the evidence does not license
text:
11.12 What the evidence does not license
The public record of the orbital environment is unusually good. ESA’s count of objects by class, the catalogue from which it can be approximated, and the concentration of who launches payloads from Sputnik to today together show the steady accumulation of debris, the steps that the 2007 test, the 2009 collision and the 2021 test cut into the record, the explosion of payloads since the large constellations began, and a concentration index that falls for decades and then climbs back — by owner state to 6,845 in 2025, by operator to 5,007, with two-thirds of the operational satellites in the catalogue belonging to one firm. They also show the decisions underneath: the dating of debris, the filtering of objects that do not orbit the Earth, the reading of owner codes, the definition of an active satellite.
Three conclusions do not follow. A rising count of objects does not tell a firm that its services are at greater risk, because risk depends on the size of objects, the shells its providers use and the manoeuvring capability of their satellites — none of which the count contains. The absence of a spike does not mean the absence of a threat: the counterspace effects firms have actually suffered — jamming, spoofing, cyberattacks on ground segments — leave no trace in a catalogue of objects. And concentration by owner code is not the firm’s dependence. A firm may buy its connectivity from a small operator in an unconcentrated market and still depend on one state’s navigation system for its time, or buy from the dominant operator through a reseller and not know it.
What the evidence does support is a conclusion about where the risk sits. Space was governed for half a century by a bargain between two states that could each destroy the other’s satellites and chose, mostly, not to. That bargain has not been replaced; it has been overlaid by a market in which one firm carries much of the world’s new capacity, by coalitions writing rules the treaty process cannot, and by an environment that the least careful user degrades for everyone. In each of those layers the risk falls less on the owner of the satellite than on the customer of the service, and the customer is usually the last to know. A multinational’s exposure to space therefore begins not with the sky but with a list it rarely keeps: the satellite services it buys, the operators and states behind each, and the regions where its ships, aircraft and sites depend on signals that someone else can switch off.

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions: What a Multinational Can Know About Geopolitical Risk
text:
12.1 The question this book began with
This book opened with a question: how does a multinational firm know how much geopolitical risk it faces, and what should it do about it? Eleven chapters later the honest answer to the first half is that it never knows, in the sense of holding a number that settles the matter, and much of the book has been an account of why. The answer to the second half is more encouraging. A firm can organise what it does not know so that someone acts on it, at the right moment, for reasons that can be stated in advance and checked afterwards. That is what a risk function is for.
This concluding chapter draws the threads together. It takes two classic contributions — Stephen Kobrin’s review of political risk, published in 1979, and Witold Henisz’s measure of political constraint, published in 2000 — and uses them to frame what the preceding chapters established: that geopolitical risk is a contingency rather than an event; that it is measured through families of indicators that disagree; that every famous figure is a stack of decisions; that the system a firm operates in moves slowly and then suddenly; that the risk reaches the firm through identifiable channels, increasingly as the instrument or the collateral of state power; and that indicators decide nothing until someone attaches a threshold, a decision and an owner to them. It ends with the question with which any analyst should end: what would change your mind?

title: 12  From Indicators to Decisions: What a Multinational Can Know About Geopolitical Risk
section: 12.2 The event is not the risk
text:
12.2 The event is not the risk
Frank Knight drew the distinction that every risk analyst still uses, even when they do not name it (Knight 1921). Risk, in his sense, is uncertainty that can be measured: the outcomes are known and their probabilities can be estimated from experience, so the uncertainty can be priced, insured or diversified. Uncertainty proper is the rest: situations unique enough, or new enough, that no frequency distribution exists. Most of what this book has called geopolitical risk is Knightian uncertainty in that sense. There is no actuarial table of invasions, no frequency distribution of secondary sanctions on a given country, no base rate for a constellation operator’s government ordering it to switch off a region. The indices examined in the preceding chapters are attempts to make the second kind of uncertainty behave a little more like the first — to give it a scale, a history and a comparison — and they do not entirely succeed.
Kobrin’s contribution, in a review written as the field of political risk assessment was taking shape, was to insist on a second distinction (Kobrin 1979). The literature he surveyed used “political risk” in two ways: some writers meant political events — instability, violence, changes of government — and others meant the effects of politics on business — expropriation, restrictions, changes in the rules. Kobrin argued that the first is not the risk. Political instability in a country is a property of that country; whether it affects a particular firm’s operations depends on the firm’s industry, its assets, its partners and its relationship with the government. A coup may leave a consumer-goods importer untouched and ruin a mining concession; a peaceful election may produce a government that rewrites the tax code for one sector. Risk lies in the contingency between the event and the firm.

Political risk (Kobrin) — not the political event itself, but the contingency that political events or conditions will affect a particular firm’s operations — its revenues, costs, assets and freedom to act. The same event carries different risks for different firms; a measure of the event is not a measure of the risk.

This book has widened Kobrin’s frame in one direction. His concern was largely with host-country risk: what the government of the country in which a firm invests might do to it. Geopolitical risk, as Chapter 1 defined it, includes the risk that originates outside the host country — in Washington, Beijing, Brussels or Moscow — and reaches the firm through its suppliers, customers, banks and networks. A sanction imposed by the firm’s home state on the country where it has a subsidiary, an export control on a component it buys, a jammer operating in a strait its ships use: none of these is a decision of the host government, and all of them reach the firm through the contingencies Kobrin described.

From the archive · Iran, 1979
Kobrin’s review appeared in the spring of 1979, in the first months of the revolution that ended the Shah’s rule in Iran. Few events have taught multinationals more about the gap between country analysis and firm risk. Iran had been a favoured destination for Western investment and contracting through the 1970s, rich with oil revenue and governed by a regime regarded as a firm ally of the United States. Its collapse cancelled contracts, stranded assets and exposed staff to danger within months.
The year ended with a second lesson. After the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, President Carter used the International Emergency Economic Powers Act — the statute on which most of the American sanctions programmes discussed in Chapter 10 still rest — to freeze Iranian government assets under US jurisdiction. Many American firms had claims against Iran. They obtained redress only through the Algiers Accords of January 1981, which ended the hostage crisis and created the Iran–United States Claims Tribunal in The Hague to arbitrate them. The firms were paid, eventually, out of the frozen assets: their risk had been settled by a negotiation between states in which they had no seat.
The episode is commonly cited as a reason so many firms built or expanded formal political risk units in the years that followed. Kobrin’s own study of how American firms organised political assessment appeared three years later (Kobrin 1982). The lesson both drew is the one this book has tried to establish: the analysis of a country is the beginning of the assessment of a firm’s risk, not the end.

Every serious assessment of geopolitical risk is therefore a claim about Kobrin’s contingency, and it starts from the firm’s footprint — where its revenue, assets, suppliers and people are. A risk report that begins with a map of the world coloured by a country index has not yet begun to assess the firm’s risk; one that begins with the firm’s own disclosures, and asks which of its countries, suppliers and channels the index bears on, has. The finding of Chapter 7, that most of the variation in political risk measured from earnings calls is specific to the firm rather than common to its country or sector (Hassan et al. 2019), is the quantitative form of the same point.
